I.

OVERVIEW

[
1
]

This trial is a perfect study of the dangers of
entering into oral agreements with close friends. It is also an unfortunate
illustration of the dangers of entering into written trust agreements without any
dates of execution noted on the document. It is perhaps an even greater example
of the difficulty with entering into oral, and then written, trust agreements
without a clear understanding of the rights and obligations of the trustee and the
beneficiaries of those trust agreements.

[
2
]

The trial was compounded by serious allegations
that all of the parties were fabricating their stories and had fabricated
documents to support their version of events. Each side says the others’
witnesses lack any credibility or reliability, and have fabricated their
stories and certain documents with the clear intention of deceiving this Court.

[
3
]

There were an untold number of applications
during the trial, starting with an application at the commencement of trial by
the defendants to withdraw admissions made in their response to civil claim.
While the trial was initially estimated to be 25 days, it ultimately resulted
in 108 days of trial, spread over almost 19 months. Each side blames the other
for the length of this unduly protracted and complicated trial.

[
4
]

The defendant, Harjinder Cheema, purchased a
property in Surrey located at 6728 – 152 St. (the “Property”) in the fall of
1996 for $690,000. The plaintiffs, Gurdarshan Mand and Kuldip Gill, were
friends of Mr. Cheema and his realtors for his purchase of the Property.
The three men agree that in 1996 they reached an oral agreement that Mr. Cheema
would purchase the Property, and that Mr. Mand and Mr. Gill would
each have the opportunity to acquire a 10% beneficial interest in the Property.
To acquire this beneficial interest, they would each have to pay 10% of the
purchase price of the Property, and 10% of all ongoing expenses for the
Property. The parties agree that their oral agreement was that Mr. Cheema
would hold legal title to the Property as trustee, for the benefit of Mr. Mand,
Mr. Gill and Mr. Cheema. While the parties agree that Mr. Gill
paid his initial 10% of the purchase price, they disagree on whether Mr. Mand
did. While Mr. Mand says he did, Mr. Cheema says he did not.

[
5
]

The three also agree that, in March 2005, they decided
to enter into a written trust agreement to formally document their arrangement.
They agree the trust agreement was executed on March 30, 2005. That, however,
is the end of their agreement as to what happened. There are two diametrically
opposed versions of what happened after that first trust agreement was executed
early in the day on March 30, 2005. The evidence adduced by the parties at
trial was centered on supporting their respective versions of the narrative.

[
6
]

The plaintiffs say they fulfilled all of their
obligations pursuant to the oral agreement and oral trust, and pursuant to the
written trust agreement executed on March 30, 2005. They say a second trust
agreement and a modification agreement were later executed, and neither affect
their beneficial interest. They say they currently have a beneficial interest
in the Property as to a total of 20%. They seek a declaration to that effect, partition
and sale of the Property and equitable damages, or alternatively, an accounting
of the profits they say Mr. Cheema has received as a result of his use of
the Property.

[
7
]

The defendants, however, say that the second
trust agreement and the modification agreement were later executed on the same
day as the first written trust agreement (on March 30, 2005). They argue that
these two documents, taken together, have the legal consequence of “nullifying”
both the oral trust agreement and the subsequent executed written trust
agreements. Further, they argue the plaintiffs failed to satisfy either the
condition precedent or the condition subsequent of the oral agreement, the oral
trust, or the executed written trust agreement, and argue their beneficial interest
in the Property was extinguished. They say the plaintiffs no longer have a beneficial
interest in the Property and all of their claims should be dismissed.

[
8
]

Unfortunately, none of the written trust
agreements had any indication of the dates they were executed. The witness
blocks failed to record when the various parties executed the trust agreements
or the modification agreement, and there is no other evidence on their face to
record that information. The lawyer’s office did not retain their files from
March 2005, nor did it retain a copy of the originally executed trust
agreements or modification agreement. In fact, only two alleged originals were
ultimately produced at trial: a version of Trust Agreement #2 and a version of
the Modification Agreement (both defined later in this judgment). I say “alleged
originals” as there was no independent evidence to corroborate either was a
fully executed original, and the most the witnesses could say was the
handwriting felt like original handwriting to them when they ran their hands
over the back of the paper. Almost every material fact at issue in this case is
in dispute. The fact-finding I must engage in is made difficult by the absence
of clear documentary evidence which supports when the respective trust deeds
were executed; it is even more so given that credibility and reliability are
major obstacles for all of the significant witnesses.

II.

APPLICATIONS AT TRIAL

[
9
]

There were an untold number of applications
during the trial. It is not necessary to detail the results of all of the
applications; however, it is necessary to briefly summarize those the parties
argue may be relevant to my final determination.

[
10
]

First, the defendants brought an application at the commencement of
the trial to withdraw admissions made in their first response to civil claim
filed July 2020, and in their first amended response to civil claim filed
August 2020. In reasons indexed as
Mand v. Cheema
,
2023 BCSC 1388
(“
Admissions
RFJ
”) I granted their application on June 21, 2023. Pursuant to my order
the defendants filed a further amended response to third amended notice of
civil claim on June 22, 2023, and then filed a further amended response to
fourth amended notice of civil claim on June 30, 2023 (the “Amended Response”).

[
11
]

Second, the parties consented to an order on
August 28, 2023, declaring that the defendants waived solicitor-client
privilege with their lawyers, namely Rajpal Binpal and Jason Sandhu, for all
matters in relation to the trust deeds.

[
12
]

Third, the plaintiffs sought production of records from Canada Post
with respect to the employment of Alamjeet Cheema, which production the
defendants opposed. On November 3, 2023, I granted the relief sought.

[
13
]

Fourth, on January 31, 2024, I ordered the defendants produce any
and all documents related to requests Mr. Cheema made to either Mr. Raj
Binpal or Binpal & Associates, related to instructions to amend trust deeds
related to the Property, or to two properties on West 16
th
Ave., on
or before December 31, 2016. I also ordered that Mr. Cheema was to make
his best efforts to obtain and produce material documents which may be in the
possession or control of his son, Rajpal Cheema, or his wife, Gurdave Cheema. I
noted that the document production of all the parties had been significantly
deficient in the litigation, and the parties had a highly unsatisfactory
approach to document disclosure. I set out a procedure for each party to send
to the other a final document request for any material documents that were
still missing, and I ordered that all parties were to provide affidavits
verifying their lists of documents.

[
14
]

Then, over the break between March and June of 2024, the plaintiffs
obtained two expert medical reports they sought to tender into evidence, which
opined on the cognitive abilities of Mr. Mand. They sought to enter these
into evidence, and their application was heard over four days in July 2024. In
reasons indexed as
Mand v. Cheema,
2024 BCSC 1701
, I dismissed their
application.

[
15
]

Finally, in July 2024, the defendants brought an application to
compel Mr. Gill to finish his cross-examination through a translator,
which the plaintiffs opposed. I dismissed this application.

III.

THE DOCUMENT AGREEMENT

[
16
]

At the commencement of trial, counsel entered into evidence a common
book of documents (three volumes) and a defendants’ common book of documents
(also three volumes). At the same time, they entered a document agreement to
record their agreement that all documents within these six volumes were authentic
and admissible at trial. Accordingly, these six volumes and the document
agreement were entered as numbered exhibits.

[
17
]

However, in the third week of trial, Mr. Taylor resiled from
the position in the document agreement that all of the documents were agreed to
be admissible evidence at trial. After consultation with counsel, I determined
the only way to deal with this issue was for counsel to agree, at the end of
the evidence, to a list of which documents in either book of documents had not
been admitted into evidence during the trial. Counsel followed this direction,
and their agreed upon lists were entered as exhibits at the end of the evidence.

IV.

DOCUMENTS IN ALLEGED NATIVE FORMAT

[
18
]

There were a few sets of documents disclosed, and entered into
evidence, which were retrieved by a witness from their computers in electronic
format. Notably, these were the files of Manpreet Mand, the files of Mr. Binpal,
and certain emails and attachments from Mr. Gill’s email account. I will
refer to Mr. Mand’s daughter Manpreet Mand as Ms. Mand, to make clear
that I am not talking of her mother, Mrs. Mand.

[
19
]

All of those documents were retrieved by way of someone inserting a
USB into the witness’ computer and copying the documents, in the format they
were saved on their computer, onto the USB. The USB sticks were then disclosed
and copied to be used at trial.

[
20
]

All counsel referred to these electronic documents as documents in
their “native format”, despite my oft-repeated comments that documents in
“native format” must be retrieved in a manner that will properly capture and disclose
the metadata of the document. It is that metadata which provides the embedded
information of the document, and may provide details such as the source, type,
owner, and date of creation of the document. See, for example,
Questor
Technology Inc. v. Stagg
,
2022 ABQB 578
at para.
114
; and
Bard v.
Canadian Natural Resources
,
2016 ABQB 267
at para.
78
.

[
21
]

During the testimony of Ms. Mand and Mr. Binpal, counsel objected
to questions arising from the properties of each document; that is, the
properties of the various Microsoft Word documents. I concluded that none of
the witnesses had captured the documents in native format. I also found that none
of them had established an evidentiary basis upon which they could give
evidence of their personal opinion of what the “properties” of the Word
documents disclosed. The difficulties of not producing the proper “native
format” of these documents were most clearly illustrated during Ms. Mand’s
direct evidence, when counsel were surprised that every time they opened a Word
document in court, the “total editing time”, as set out in the properties, had changed.

[
22
]

I did not accept the properties of the Word documents as metadata,
nor did I accept that any of these sets of documents had been produced in
native format.

V.

PROPER SCOPE OF REPLY

[
23
]

At the beginning of the plaintiffs’ reply, counsel for the
defendants made an unexpected argument that the majority of the reply was
inappropriate. I say unexpected as this matter has been diligently case managed
since June 2023, and the exchange of written closing submissions, as well as
the length of time for oral closing submissions (including reply), were set
with counsel. Further to my directions, counsel engaged in an orderly exchange
of written closing arguments, including the plaintiffs’ reply, well in advance
of the oral hearing. No objection to the plaintiffs’ written reply was made by
the defendants at the start of the three weeks of oral closing argument.

[
24
]

In the interests of efficiency, I allowed counsel to argue the
objection, and I allowed the plaintiffs to argue their reply orally. I noted that
I would address the allowable scope of the plaintiffs’ reply in my reasons for
judgment.

[
25
]

Counsel for the defendants argues that because this case was
judicially managed, and I directed the orderly exchange of written submissions
in advance of oral submissions, then the plaintiffs properly ought to have
addressed anything arising from the defendants’ written submissions in their
oral closing submissions. Counsel says they should be limited in their oral and
written reply to anything new the defendants addressed orally in closing
submissions. They rely upon a decision of the federal court in
Merck-Frosst v.
Canada (Health)
,
2009 FC 914
at paras.
29–30
. I note that this case
deals with a motion to file reply evidence, which is not what I must address.

[
26
]

The proper scope of reply “is to respond to matters raised by the
opposing party, not to produce new arguments or new evidence that should have
been raised in first instance”:
Deegan v. Canada (Attorney General
),

2019 FC 960
at para.
121
.

[
27
]

All counsel rely upon the decision of Justice L.
Smith (as she then was) in
Carter v. Canada (Attorney General)
,
2012
BCSC 886
, aff’d
2015 SCC 5
[
Carter
] at paras.
148
–
159. Specifically, they agree Justice Smith accurately
summarized the proper scope of reply when stating:

[152]  The
plaintiffs argue that they anticipated and addressed the defendants’ argument
to the extent reasonably possible in their detailed argument in chief. However,
they submit, they are entitled to reply to Canada’s submissions, including the
ways in which Canada relies upon and interprets the evidence.

[
28
]

As in
Carter
, were I to accept the defendants’ theory of
reply, it would require the plaintiffs to anticipate the defendants’ entire
theory of the case and rebut it in advance of hearing it, while putting forward
their own theory of the case at the same time: at para. 154. That is not
necessary, nor appropriate, even for long trials with vigilant case management.

[
29
]

I am satisfied the plaintiffs did not tender any new evidence in
their reply submissions; although they did refer to specific evidence that, in
their view, responded to the evidence upon which the defendants relied. I am
also satisfied they did not advance any new theories of the case, nor any new
arguments, that were not responsive to arguments raised by the defendants. I am
satisfied that, in the circumstances of this case, the plaintiffs’ reply is
proper reply under both the
Supreme Court Civil Rules
and practice of this
Court, and I receive their written and oral reply submissions into evidence.

VI.

BRIEF BACKGROUND

[
30
]

The parties are largely in agreement on the events in 1996
surrounding the purchase of the Property. Mr. Mand and Mr. Gill were
realtors, and were friends of Mr. Cheema.

[
31
]

They introduced the Property to Mr. Cheema. The Property was
subject to a foreclosure. Ultimately, Mr. Cheema’s contract of purchase
and sale was accepted for a purchase price of $690,000.00. Mr. Cheema paid
the deposit of $20,000.00 by way of cheque dated August 6, 1996. A court order
approving the sale was made on August 14, 1996, and, subsequently, the vendor
removed the subject clause for court approval of the sale.

[
32
]

Mr. Cheema paid the $20,000.00 deposit for the Property by way
of a cheque made out on his Vancity account #64873 (“Vancity #64873”). On
August 14, 1996, his balance in that account was $8,121.59.

[
33
]

The parties disagree as to when the idea was raised that Mr. Mand
and Mr. Gill would participate as investors in the Property. Mr. Cheema
says it was raised before he put forward his offer to purchase the Property, but
Mr. Mand and Mr. Gill say it was only raised after the removal of the
subject clause requiring court approval of the sale. There is no independent
documentary evidence to resolve this dispute. I am satisfied it is not
necessary to resolve this dispute to determine the issues that arise in this
litigation.

[
34
]

In any event, the parties do agree that, around the time Mr. Cheema
purchased the Property, they reached an oral agreement that Mr. Cheema
would hold legal title to the Property in trust for the beneficial owners of
the Property, being: Mr. Mand as to a 10% beneficial interest; Mr. Gill
as to a 10% beneficial interest; and Mr. Cheema as to an 80% beneficial
interest. The parties agree that the terms of that oral agreement were:

a)

Mr. Mand and Mr. Gill were to pay Mr. Cheema their
respective 10% capital contribution for the acquisition of the Property;

b)

Mr. Mand and Mr. Gill were to pay Mr. Cheema their
respective 10% of the ongoing expenses related to the Property;

c)

Mr. Mand and Mr. Gill would be responsible for renting out
the small home on the Property (the “Home”); and

d)

Mr. Cheema would hold legal title to the Property pursuant to an
oral trust, on the basis of the above terms,

(collectively, the
“Agreement”).

While the parties referred to the Agreement
in a number of ways, including an oral trust and an oral agreement, I shall
refer to it as the Agreement. I note both parties from time to time referred to
the “oral trust”, which was one term of the Agreement. I will refer as
appropriate to the “oral trust”, when referring to that term of the Agreement
that Mr. Cheema would hold legal title to the Property as Trustee,
pursuant to the terms of the Agreement.

[
35
]

Mr. Cheema’s lawyer, Wayne Buckley, provided him with a
Statement of Adjustments as of September 19, 1996, which set out the balance
required for completion as $385,376.76. The parties agree that the capital
contribution required from Mr. Mand and Mr. Gill for their 10% was
$40,537.67 (being 10% of the total of the amount for completion plus the
$20,000.00 deposit). Mr. Cheema obtained a mortgage from Laurentian Trust
in the amount of $299,282.78. Mr. Cheema also had a bank account in his
name at Laurentian Bank associated with the Property (the “Laurentian Account”).

[
36
]

Mr. Cheema acknowledges that Mr. Gill paid him his 10%
share for the capital contribution for the purchase of the Property by way of a
bank draft dated September 13, 1996 in the amount of $40,537.67. Mr. Gill
has produced a copy of his bank draft which proves this payment. However, while
both Mr. Mand and Mr. Gill maintain Mr. Mand also paid the
identical amount, he has no documentation to corroborate his evidence. This
became a central issue at trial.

[
37
]

Mr. Cheema’s son, Rajpal Cheema, guaranteed
the mortgage required for the purchase of the Property. Mr. Buckley’s
statement of account, dated September 17, 1996, records the specific legal
services provided with respect to this guarantee as follows:

LEGAL FEES, for
all professional services rendered with respect to the above, including … ;
receiving mortgage instructions from Laurentian Bank and noting that your son,
Rajpal Cheema was to sign as a Covenantor under Independent Legal advice;
…telephone conversation with Gary Mand who advised that he would arrange the
Independent Legal Advice for Rajpal Cheema; … letter to Gary Mand enclosing
copy of Mortgage and supporting documents for Rajpal Cheema to sign with
instructions that the documents be returned to our office as soon as this has
been done; …

[
38
]

As noted above, the parties are also in general agreement that,
pursuant to the Agreement, Mr. Gill and Mr. Mand were to take care of
all of the arrangements for renting out the Home and depositing the rental
income in the Property’s bank account. They agree Mr. Gill was primarily
responsible for depositing these rental cheques. Mr. Gill takes the
position that he dutifully deposited all of the rental cheques he obtained,
although he acknowledges he has not been able to find a complete record of all
of the deposits he made. He initially made the deposits into the Laurentian Account,
and after the mortgage was transferred to Vancity in February 2002, into the
Vancity #136473 account (“Vancity #136473”). Mr. Cheema says he gave the
Laurentian Account statements to the plaintiffs without looking at them. Mr. Gill
and Mr. Mand deny ever receiving these statements.

[
39
]

Mr. Cheema takes the position that Mr. Gill has failed to
keep appropriate records, and he cannot prove that he deposited all of the
rental proceeds. Mr. Cheema also has not been able to provide a full set
of the relevant bank account records for the period from September 1996 to
March 2005, and so, cannot provide a full record of all the funds he received
from Mr. Mand and Mr. Gill.

[
40
]

On February 28, 2002, the mortgage on the Property was transferred
from Laurentian Bank to Vancity Bank. At the time, the mortgage balance was
$262,203.98.

[
41
]

On April 9, 2003, Mr. Cheema granted a
second mortgage to Vancity, securing a $220,000 line of credit. At this time,
the principal balance on the mortgage had been reduced to $247,313.80.

[
42
]

The plaintiffs say that in approximately 2004 Mr. Cheema ceased
to request payments from Mr. Mand and Mr. Gill on account of the net
cash flow deficiency, and, instead, told them he had decided to manage the
income and expenses of the Property through Vancity #136473 and the line of
credit. They say their final payments to the cash flow deficiencies were made
on June 30, 2004, in the amount of $2,500.00 each. Mr. Gill provided a
copy of a cheque made out in this amount, and Mr. Mand produced a copy of
a cheque register recording a cheque made out in the same amount, on the same
day, to Mr. Cheema, with the notation of “6728 – 152 St”. The plaintiffs
also point to a statement from July 2004 for Vancity #136473 showing a deposit
of $5,000.00 on July 7, 2004.

[
43
]

Mr. Cheema, however, says that at that approximate time, he
began to be concerned that Mr. Gill and Mr. Mand had not paid their
proportionate share of the expenses incurred for the Property, nor of the
“ongoing shortfall”, and he began to undertake a financial investigation to try
to determine the Property’s “true state of [financial] affairs”. He conducted a
reconciliation of the funds he said they still owed him. While he testified that
he had a page on which these investigations were summarized, he was not able to
produce it for the purposes of litigation. However, he testified that according
to his reconciliation, Mr. Mand still owed him his capital contribution of

$40,537.67
, and each of Mr. Mand and Mr. Gill
owed him approximately $40,000.00 for the ongoing expenses related to the
Property. Mr. Cheema testified that he advised Mr. Mand and Mr. Gill
of this. Both deny he ever said such a thing.

[
44
]

In any event, Mr. Cheema testified that in March 2005 he
decided it would be prudent to arrange for a written trust agreement to
document the Agreement. He discussed this with Mr. Mand and Mr. Gill,
and they agreed. He told them that he wanted to add certain beneficiaries to
benefit from his 80%. They had no problem with this, but they each wished to
add their wives to benefit from their respective 10% shares. Similarly, Mr. Cheema
had no problem with this request. Accordingly, Mr. Cheema instructed his
lawyer, Mr. Binpal, to prepare such a written trust agreement.

[
45

A.

Applicable Evidentiary Principles

1.

The Plaintiffs’ Burden of Proof

[
107
]

It is trite to state that the plaintiffs bear the burden to prove
their case. In circumstances where a trial judge cannot determine whose version
of events is most probably true, then the consideration becomes who has the
burden of proof on that specific issue. Counsel are not in disagreement on this
proposition.

[
108
]

However, it is important to remember the plaintiffs do not bear the
burden of refuting the defendants’ version of events. Rather, the defendants
bear the burden of proving the events they rely upon to establish a defence on
a balance of probabilities. If they are able to do so, then the plaintiffs bear
the burden of proving any events they say are relevant in response to the
defendants’ version of events.

[
109
]

I raise this because who bears the onus of proof is relevant to my
analysis, particularly given the serious difficulties Mr. Mand, Mr. Gill
and Mr. Cheema all have with their credibility.

[
110
]

In these circumstances, the plaintiffs must prove on a balance of
probabilities:

a)

the parties entered into the Agreement in 1996 that Mr. Cheema
would hold legal title to the Property in trust for the beneficiaries, which
included Mr. Mand and Mr. Cheema;

b)

Mr. Mand and Mr. Cheema satisfied the condition precedent
to the Agreement and paid their capital contribution; and

c)

the parties entered into Trust Agreement #1 on March 30, 2005.

[
111
]

If the plaintiffs establish the above on a balance of probabilities,
then the burden shifts to Mr. Cheema to prove that Trust Agreement #2 was
also executed on March 30, 2005 and was either “nullified” by the Modification
Agreement (allegedly executed on the same day), or was otherwise terminated by Mr. Cheema
in a legally enforceable manner.

2.

Credibility and Reliability of Witnesses

[
112
]

There is no doubt that credibility is a central issue in this case.
Significant credibility issues arose for Mr. Cheema, Mr. Mand and Mr. Gill
as a result of changes in their evidence from their examinations for discovery
to trial, the nature and manner of their responses to questioning at trial
(including but not limited to their demeanour and behaviour in the courtroom),
their clear revision of their testimony to “fit” with newly disclosed documents
and new theories of the case, the overall plausibility of their evidence, and the
significant conflicts in the evidence of these three men. The assessment of
credibility was made even more difficult with the lack of many contemporaneous
independent documents, particularly the lack of documents confirming when Trust
Agreement #1, Trust Agreement #2 (both with Schedule A with the old PID and
Schedule A with the new PID), and the Modification Agreement were fully
executed.

[
113
]

I am conscious of the principles set out in the leading authorities
concerning the manner in which a trial judge should assess credibility and
reliability, including:
Youyi Group Holdings (Canada) Ltd. v. Brentwood
Lanes Canada Ltd.,
2019 BCSC 739
[
Youyi
], appeal dismissed
2020 BCCA
130
; Bradshaw v. Stenner
,
2010 BCSC 1398
[
Bradshaw
], aff’d 2012
BCCA 296, leave to appeal ref’d [2012] S.C.C.A. No. 392; and
Faryna v.
Chorny
,
1951 CanLII 252 (BC CA)
, [1952] 2 D.L.R. 354 (B.C.C.A.).

[
114
]

The determination of the credibility and reliability of a witness
requires the trial judge to make an assessment of their evidence. It is not an
all or nothing proposition, and I may ultimately decide to accept some, all, or
none of a witness’ evidence. I may attach different weight to different parts
of that evidence:
Radacina v. Aquino
,
2020 BCSC 1143
at para.
96
. A
credibility assessment requires the trial judge to consider the trustworthiness
of a witness’ testimony, based upon the sincerity of a witness and the accuracy
of their evidence. A lack of credibility may be found as a result of a
determination that a witness has made a conscious decision not to tell the truth,
or for some other reason they are unable to provide an honest account of
historic events. A lack of reliability may be found as a result of the
conclusion that their evidence is not accurate. Credibility relates to the
honesty of the witness, while reliability relates to the accuracy of their
evidence, which engages a consideration of their ability to accurately observe,
recall and recount the events in issue. A witness who is not credible cannot
give reliable evidence, whereas a credible witness may give unreliable
evidence. Credibility is not a proxy for reliability:
R. v. H.C.,
2009
ONCA 56
at para.
41
.

[
115
]

A useful methodology to the assessment of credibility was
articulated at paras. 186–187 of
Bradshaw
. First, I am to consider
the testimony of a witness on a “stand alone” basis, followed by an analysis of
whether their story is inherently believable. If their evidence has survived
relatively intact, then I must evaluate their evidence based upon its
consistency with other witnesses and documentary evidence, and the testimony of
non-party, disinterested witnesses, which may provide a reliable yardstick for
comparison. Finally, I must determine which version of events is the most
consistent with the preponderance of probabilities which a practical and informed
person would readily recognize as reasonable in that place and in those
conditions.

[
116
]

A determination of what is “inherently
believable” or “reasonable” may, in some circumstances, be a subjective
assessment which reflects personal experience. Accordingly, it may be
unintentionally informed by implicit bias, and even by inappropriate
stereotyping or myths:
Phoenix Homes Limited v. Takhar
,
2023 BCSC 184
[
Phoenix
Homes
] at para.
63
. This may be true in cases involving the testimony
of witnesses from different cultures and backgrounds, and witnesses testifying
through an interpreter: at para. 63. Special care must be taken to ensure
difficulties with providing evidence through an interpreter are not equated
with evasiveness:
Fu v. Zhu
,
2018 BCSC 9
at paras.
39–42
. However,
any such inappropriate stereotyping or inherent difficulties in testifying
through an interpreter must be specifically identified by the parties.

[
117
]

While I have taken into account the potential difficulties
inherent in testifying through an interpreter, or in testifying in a second
language, in assessing the credibility of the party witnesses in this case, counsel
provided no argument that any of the party witnesses’ substantial difficulties
were rooted in these factors. Further, any such difficulties do not provide a
license for a witness to lie. This caution cannot diminish a truthful witness,
nor elevate an untruthful witness:
Kim v. Choi
,
2019 BCSC 437
at para.
18
,
aff’d
2020 BCCA 98
. Neither did counsel identify any specific impermissible
myths or stereotypes I should be cautious of in these circumstances.

[
118
]

As noted above, a consideration of credibility involves a
consideration of the witness’ account of events and its consistency with other
admissible evidence from other witnesses or documents, and whether the witness’
evidence is reliably corroborated or contradicted by this other evidence.
However, in this case, there is a paucity of independent documentary evidence
and third-party witnesses.

[
119
]

In
Youyi
,
Justice Mayer (as he then was) set out a helpful
summary of additional factors which may impact credibility: at para. 92. I
find the following are relevant in this matter:

a)

a series of inconsistencies, when considered in their totality, may
become quite significant and cause the trier of fact to have a reasonable doubt
about the reliability of the witness’ testimony;

b)

credibility will be undermined when a party has failed to produce
documents;

c)

credibility will be in doubt when a witness’ explanation defies
business logic or common sense; and

d)

credibility may be impacted when a witness is evasive, longwinded
and argumentative in their responses to questions.

[
120
]

On the issue of the impact on the assessment of the credibility of a
witness for failing to produce relevant documents, documents created
contemporaneously will often provide the most accurate reflection of what
occurred, particularly with respect to historic events. Memories can fade with
time, become hardened through the adversarial process, or be reconstructed for
a variety of reasons and then presented as accurate evidence:
Bradshaw

at
para.
188
. The plaintiffs argue that
Bradshaw
stands for the
proposition that the inability to produce relevant documents is a factor that
negatively affects credibility. They rely upon Justice Dillon’s comment “[t]he
inability to produce relevant documents to support one’s case is also a
relevant factor that negatively affects credibility”: at para. 188. While
the defendants argue that this statement must be limited to failing to produce
only relevant documents that would support one’s own case, I cannot agree. In a
case such as this, with an unfortunate lack of relevant, contemporaneous
documents, I find the inability to produce material documents at one time in a
party’s care and control that would support the other party’s case is also a
relevant factor, particularly where a party can inexplicably produce documents
to support their own case.

[
121
]

In a similar manner, the parties agree that a determination that a
party produced a falsified document may be severely damaging to the credibility
of that party:
Osayande v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration)
,

2002 FCT 368
at paras.
19–21
. While the plaintiffs argue this would hold
true if a party merely produces false documents, I am satisfied there must be
some evidence that the party either created the false document, or produced it
knowing it was falsified, before such a determination is appropriate.

[
122
]

While the fact that a witness has previously
lied, even under oath, does not require a finding that he or she lacks
credibility in all respects, the fact that a witness has been found to have
lied during trial will be a key consideration:
Virk v. Singh
,
2020 BCSC
225
at para.
67
, aff’d
2022 BCCA 153
[
Virk BCCA
]. A consideration
of the context, and any justification for the false or misleading statements,
is required. However, as the Court stated in
Moinzadeh v. Loblaws Inc.,

2021 BCSC 793
:

[17] Sometimes,
however, witnesses deliberately lie and intend to deceive. When that occurs, it
may be impossible to accurately separate truth from falsehood and the court may
simply find the witness’s testimony wholly unreliable. The more frequently the
witness lies, the more likely that will be the case. If as a consequence a
truth is not accepted as a fact by the court, the witness has only himself or
herself to blame.

[
123
]

If a party “practises to deceive” the Court, whether it be by lying
or gross exaggeration, it causes significant difficulty for the trier of fact
to disentangle the truth from the “web of deceit and exaggeration”:
Le
(Guardian ad litem of) v. Milburn,
[1987] B.C.J. No. 2690, 1987
CarswellBC 1589 (S.C.) [
Milburn
] at 2
. Again, if the result is the court
casts aside something that was true, the party has only himself to blame.

[
124
]

Finally, in circumstances where the court is left in the difficult
position where no party has been found to be credible, I must still consider
whether it is possible to find the necessary facts underlying the plaintiffs’
claim. As listed by this Court in
Qi v. Qin,
2024 BCSC 1830
[
Qi
]
that will involve a consideration of the undisputed facts; the objective
documentary evidence; an absence of contradictory evidence; common sense and
commercial reasonableness; any inferences that are drawn (adverse or
reasonable); and the available independent evidence: at para. 63. It will
also require a consideration of my assessment of the probabilities affecting
the case as a whole: at para. 63.

[
125
]

If the state of the evidence is such that a finding of fact cannot
fairly or properly be made, then the matter may ultimately be determined based
on the burden of proof, and the trial judge may determine the plaintiff has failed
to discharge their burden:
Phoenix Homes

at para.
68
; see also
Silverhill
Homes Ltd. v. Borowski
,
2019 BCCA 227
at para.
42
.

[
126
]

The plaintiffs rely heavily on the testimony of Mr. Mand and Mr. Gill,
as well as the testimony of their wives and of Ms. Mand. The defendants place
significant reliance on the testimony of Mr. Cheema, as well as his family
members, and his lawyers Mr. Binpal and Mr. Sandhu.

[
127
]

In this case, I have significant concerns about the credibility of Mr. Mand,
Mr. Gill and Mr. Cheema. I find that all three lacked credibility and
reliability. Their evidence on key factual points conflicted, and must be
scrutinised with particular care. Their respective testimony was frequently contradictory,

[
128
]

I have taken special care to ensure I do not
equate any difficulties with providing evidence in this case through either an
interpreter (for Mr. Cheema and Mr. Mand), or through a second
language (for Mr. Gill), to be conclusive of evasiveness.

[
129
]

I will address in detail the difficulties inherent in their evidence
in due course. At this point, it is enough to say that I cannot accept Mr. Mand’s
evidence, as I find he lacked credibility and reliability. Further, I accept Mr. Cheema
and Mr. Gill’s evidence only to the extent that it is corroborated by either

Youyi

at
para.
101
.

3.

Inferences
—
Reasonable and Adverse

[
130
]

A party is not limited to proving his or her case with oral and
documentary evidence. They may also be able to do so with a reasonable factual
inference made upon circumstantial evidence, or by an adverse inference.

[
131
]

Turning first to the approach required to draw a reasonable
inference on the basis of circumstantial evidence, Justice Williams set out a
helpful summary of the proper approach in
Paguio v. Fraser
,
2011 BCSC
1519
[
Paguio
] at para.
61
, which I would summarize as:

a)

where a case is not proven by direct evidence, the court is to
carefully examine and consider the relevant circumstantial evidence;

b)

reasonable inferences may be made from circumstantial evidence,
where a trial judge determines that a logical conclusion can be drawn from
certain facts that have been proven;

c)

a reasonable inference must not be mere conjecture or guess work, no
matter “how shrewd or plausible that guess might be”;

d)

a reasonable inference must give rise to reasonable conviction in
the mind of the trial judge “that the element of which proof is necessary is at
least more likely than not”; and

e)

a plaintiff can succeed in proving her case on the strength of a
reasonable inference.

[
132
]

Drawing a reasonable inference “is the process
of reasoning from a proven fact or facts to a reasonable, rational and
logically legitimate conclusion”:
Paguio
at para.
61
(b). The
decision of whether it is appropriate to make such an inference is governed by
the application of logic, common sense and experience to the totality of the
evidence:
British Columbia (Director of Civil Forfeiture) v. Angel Acres Recreation
and Festival Property Ltd.
,
2023 BCCA 70
[
Angel Acres
] at para.
172
.
It cannot be mere speculation or conjecture. If the inference does not flow
logically and reasonably from established facts, it cannot be drawn: at para. 172.
However, as the Court of Appeal makes clear, if evidence may support more than
one inference, the trial judge must determine whether the evidence establishes
particular factual inferences on a balance of probabilities: at para. 174.
It “is only in the case of inconsistency between such available inferences –
namely, where the two inferences cannot both be true – that the trier of fact
must determine which is more probable”: at para. 174. The Court goes on to
clarify:

[176] By contrast, in a civil case, “a judge
may choose among any number of available reasonable inferences”:
Rain Coast
Water Corp.
at para. 69. As the defendants acknowledge, it would be an
error for a trial judge in a civil case to require a party to disprove all
other rational inferences arising from circumstantial evidence (assuming of
course that those other inferences are not inconsistent with the invited
inference). That would be tantamount to applying the criminal standard of
proof.

[177] In a civil case, circumstantial
evidence is treated like any other piece of evidence; “[t]he weight accorded to
it depends on the strength of the inference that can be drawn from it”: Sidney
Lederman, Michelle Fuerst & Hamish Stewart, eds.,
Sopinka, Lederman
& Bryant: The Law of Evidence in Canada
, 6
th
ed. (Toronto:
LexisNexis Canada, 2022) at 82.

[178] The fact
that a party adduces evidence from which the judge is invited to draw an
inference does not shift the burden of proof to the opposing party:
Snell v.
Farrell
, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 311 at 219 – 330,
1990 CanLII 70
. The opposing
party has a choice. It may choose to adduce its own evidence on the point, but
it is not obliged to do so. It is for that party to assess its risk in deciding
whether or not to adduce evidence. Once all the evidence is in, the trier of
fact will weigh it and determine whether to draw the invited inference. In
doing so, a judge will ordinarily consider alternative available inferences
before deciding whether to draw the invited inference.

[
133
]

Where I make a reasonable inference I will explain the basis upon
which I do so at the appropriate place in my analysis.

[
134
]

By contrast, an adverse inference is a factual determination drawn
against a party on the basis that a party has undermined the opposing party’s
ability to adduce relevant evidence or failed to provide evidence over which it
had exclusive control, without sufficient explanation:
Angel Acres

at para.
180
.
The plaintiffs ask that I draw a number of adverse inferences, arising out of
the defendants’ failure to call and adduce evidence from:

a)

Harchet Kaler and Inder Dhaliwal, both of whom are alleged to have
been present and to have witnessed documents at Mr. Cheema’s office on
March 30, 2005;

b)

Sandeep Jawandha, a friend of Mr. Cheema’s, allegedly involved
in transactions related to the 16
th
Ave. Properties (addressed
below);

c)

Mr. Cheema’s appraiser Henry Wang, who prepared appraisal
reports for Mr. Cheema in 2016 and 2020;

d)

Anurag Saini, a paralegal (now lawyer) who acted for Mr. Cheema
in 2016; and

e)

Mr. Cheema’s former counsel in 2020, whom Mr. Cheema says
misconstrued his instructions when making critical admissions in the
defendants’ first response to civil claim filed July
2020, and in their first amended response to civil claim filed August 2020.

[
135
]

The adverse inference rule is a discretionary
rule of evidence that permits the Court to draw an adverse inference against a
party by reason of his or her failure to call a witness who could be expected
to give material evidence in their favour at trial:
Angel Acres

at para.
182
;

Singh v. Reddy
,
2019 BCCA 79
at para.
1
[
Singh
]. The adverse
inference rule is discretionary, and a trial judge is not obliged to draw an
adverse inference:
Singh

at para.
9
.

[
136
]

At para. 183 of
Angel Acres
, the
Court of Appeal noted that the process of drawing an adverse inference requires
the trial judge to consider the following factors from
Singh
:

•

whether there is a legitimate explanation for
the failure to call the witness;

•

whether the witness is within the “exclusive
control” of the party, or was equally available to both parties; and

•

whether the witness has key evidence to provide
or is the best person to provide the evidence in question.

[
137
]

Of further importance, the Court clarified the
requirement that an adverse inference is not to be drawn unless a
prima
facie
case is established: see
Thomasson v. Moeller
,
2016 BCCA 14
at
para.
35
. Specifically, the Court in
Angel Acres

made clear:

[184]  If a party has not adduced sufficient
evidence to support an invited adverse inference, no adverse inference will be
drawn even if the opposing party has not called a material witness under its
control. For example, a judge will refuse to draw an adverse inference against
a party for failing to call evidence if that party did not need to call
evidence to meet the case against it: see, for example,
Insurance
Corporation of British Columbia v. Mehat
,
2018 BCCA 242
at para.

My Lords, I have
always understood that if you intend to impeach a witness you are bound, whilst
he is in the box, to give him an opportunity of making any explanation which is
open to him; and, as it seems to me, that is not only a rule of professional
practice in the conduct of a case, but is essential to fair play and fair

possible to recall the witness, then the trial judge may exercise their

62. The Plaintiffs are barred in Equity,
including by way of estoppel, laches and/or waiver from now, all these years
later, claiming that these acts or omissions constitute breach of trust, breach

63. At all
material times, the Plaintiffs have known, or reasonably ought to have known,
all the material facts relating to the claims made herein, and therefore all
such claims relating to acts, omissions or events from more than two years
before the filing of the Notice of Civil Claim are time barred by the
provisions of the
Limitation Act
, S.B.C., 2012, c.13.

[
188
]

In their closing submissions, the defendants argued the plaintiffs’
claim was barred pursuant to the application of the appropriate limitation
period. They also argued that “the position of the Defendants ought not to be
defeated by application of the doctrines of laches or estoppel”. They did not
make any arguments based on waiver. Accordingly, that is the manner in which I
will consider their arguments.

[
189
]

Section 6
of the
Limitation Act
, S.B.C., 2012, c. 13 [
Limitation
Act
] provides the basic limitation period is two years after the day on
which the claim is discovered.

[
190
]

For a trust claim,
s. 12
of the
Limitation Act

states,
for the purpose of triggering the running of a limitation date, the claim is
deemed to have been discovered when a beneficiary is fully aware that injury,
loss or damage has occurred. The onus a proving that a trust claim has been
discovered rests on the trustee:
s. 12(3)
.

[
191
]

The previous
Limitation Act

provided for a limitation period
of 10 years:
Limitation Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 266, s. 3 and

s. 6
.

[
192
]

In
Vandenbosch v. Vandenbosch,
32 B.C.L.R. (2d) 190,
1988
CanLII 3199 (BC CA)
at para.
13
, the Court, when considering this previous
statute, noted that a limitation period would commence when a trustee refused
to acknowledge he was holding the property in trust for the plaintiff. In
Lennox
v. Lennox
,
2019 BCSC 938
, Justice Horsman (as she then was), in considering
the
Limitation Act
, found the triggering event to be the point in time
the beneficiary “became fully aware that the respondent denied existence of the

at para. 46.

[
193
]

As noted by Justice Iyer (as she then was) in
Ali
v. Ali
,
2022 BCSC 1022
:

[21]  The burden
of proof of discoverability rests on the trustee, in this case, Imran: s. 12(3).
This is a more stringent test than the basic discoverability rule because the
trustee must show that the beneficiary actually “knew”, not merely that they
“ought to have known” that their claim was being denied:
Maussion v.
Maussion
,
2021 BCSC 530
at para.
35
. The purpose of the test is to
protect a dishonest trustee from obtaining the protection of a limitation
period:
Hochsteiner v. Kilback
,
2013 BCSC 1316
at para.
33
.

[
194
]

The case law makes clear that, under either statute, a limitation
period starts to run when an act occurred on the part of the trustee
inconsistent with the beneficiary’s interest:
Ghag v. United Steel
Paper and Forestry, Rubber, Manufacturing, Energy, Allied Industrial
and Service Workers International Union Local
2009
,
2022 BCCA 360
at para.
65
.

2.

Analysis

[
195
]

The defendants argue that the plaintiffs
discovered their claim in 2005 when Mr. Cheema explicitly informed them
that if they did not pay the required monies, they would not be a part of the

has proven on a balance of probabilities that he explicitly told the plaintiffs
they would no longer be a participant in the investment in the Property in
March 2005. This argument fails.

[
196
]

In the alternative, they say that the plaintiffs
became fully aware of their cause of action in 2014 when Mr. Cheema
refused to give the plaintiffs their alleged share of the truck parking
revenue; refused to execute the amendment to Trust Agreement #1 prepared by Ms. Mand;
and failed to take any steps to buy out the plaintiffs’ interest in the
Property, and so, say their claim is statute barred by virtue of
s. 6
of
the
Limitation Act
.

[
197
]

This ignores the fact that Mr. Gill produced an email dated
July 19, 2016, which establishes he was in possession of a copy of an appraisal
Mr. Wang conducted for Mr. Cheema dated April 8, 2016. I accept the
defendants’ argument that Mr. Cheema’s recorded intention “to use this
appraisal report to assist with determining a selling price between partners”

draw the adverse inference sought by the plaintiffs, who argue Mr. Wang

forwarded this appraisal to Mr. Mand and to Mr. Cheema on July 19,

[
198
]

The plaintiffs led a great deal of evidence
about a meeting with Mr. Cheema at a Tim Hortons restaurant in late 2019,
when they raised the issue of an account of net truck parking revenues, as well
as the potential buyout of their interests. Mr. Cheema denies he was in

[
199
]

That is because it is clear from the evidentiary
record that the defendants, in their first response to
civil claim filed July 2020, and in their first amended response to civil claim
filed August 2020, admitted Mr. Cheema held the Property in trust for the

Admissions RFJ
was issued
in June 2023, the plaintiffs cannot be found to have been fully aware that Mr. Cheema denied existence of the trust. Put
another way, Mr. Cheema, as Trustee, cannot now attempt to completely

C.

What was the nature, and terms, of the oral
agreement made in 1996 by Mr. Cheema, Mr. Mand and Mr. Gill with
respect to the Property?

1.

Applicable Legal Principles

[
200
]

As a starting point, it is helpful to consider what a trust is. The
following definition comes from Donovan W.M. Waters, Q.C., Mark R. Gillen &
Lionel D. Smith,
Waters’ Law of Trusts in Canada,
5
th

ed. (Toronto: Thomson Reuters Canada Limited, 2021) [
Waters’

Law of
Trusts
] at 4:

…And among lawyers of the common law
tradition the following definition is generally regarded as being one of the
best:

A trust is the
relationship which arises whenever a person (called the trustee) is compelled
in equity to hold property, whether real or personal, and whether by legal or
equitable title, for the benefit of some persons (of whom he may be one, and
who are termed beneficiaries) or for some object permitted by law, in such a
way that the real benefit of the property accrues, not to the trustees, but to
the beneficiaries or other objects of the trust.

Another familiar definition, and one that
has been cited with judicial approval, is:

A trust is an equitable fiduciary
obligation, binding a person (called a trustee) to deal with property (called
trust property) owned and controlled by him as a separate fund, distinct from
his own private property, for the benefit of persons (called beneficiaries or,
in old cases,
cestuis que trust
), of whom he may himself be one, and any
one of whom may enforce the obligation.

[
201
]

Section 23(2)
of the
Land Title Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 250
provides that indefeasible title is conclusive evidence at law and in equity
that the registered owner is indefeasibly entitled to ownership of the land
described in the title. It is a statutory presumption “whereby the registered
owner is presumed to hold their legal or equitable interest to an estate in fee
simple”, unless the statutory presumption is rebutted:
Freeland v. Farrell
,

2021 BCSC 1318
[
Freeland
] at para.
34
, aff’d on this point
2022
BCCA 99
at para.
42
.

[
202
]

The presumption of indefeasibility may be rebutted in three
circumstances:

a)

through the operation of a resulting trust which may be inferred
where no value is given for a legal interest;

b)

through the operation of an agreement between the parties that is
contrary to the registered legal title; or

c)

taking into account the underlying equitable interests between the
parties (e.g. considerations that arise in claims for unjust enrichment).

Freeland
at para.
36
.

[
203
]

Section 59(3)
of the
Law and Equity Act,
R.S.B.C.
1996, c. 253 [
Law and Equity Act
], provides:

(3) A contract respecting land or a
disposition of land is not enforceable unless

(a) there is, in a
writing signed by the party to be charged or by that party’s agent, both an
indication that it has been made and a reasonable indication of the subject
matter,

(b) the party to
be charged has done an act, or acquiesced in an act of the party alleging the
contract or disposition, that indicates that a contract or disposition not
inconsistent with that alleged has been made, or

(c)
the person
alleging the contract or disposition has, in reasonable reliance on it, so
changed the person’s position that an inequitable result, having regard to both
parties’ interest, can be avoided only by enforcing the contract or
disposition.

[Emphasis
added.]

[
204
]

A party to an oral agreement respecting land is prevented from using
a lack of a written agreement as a defence when they themselves have acted as
though there was a binding contract or the other party has detrimentally relied
on the oral agreement:
Le Soleil Hotel & Suites Ltd. v. Le Soleil
Management Inc.,
2009 BCSC 1303
at paras.
342–345
[
Le Soleil
].

[
205
]

An agreement does not have to be in writing. It may be evidenced by
writing, orally, by conduct, or by a combination of some or all of these. The
fundamental issue is whether an agreement has been reached by the parties on
all of the essential terms of the agreement. An enforceable agreement is
reached where two or more parties have reached a manifest meeting of the minds.
The parties must express themselves outwardly in a manner that indicates an
intention to be bound, and there must be reasonably certain mutually agreed
upon terms:
Le Soleil

at paras.
322–323
; see also
Wong v. Wong
,

2024 BCSC 1305
[
Wong
] at paras.
241 and 247
.

[
206
]

In determining the terms of an oral contract, it
may be that the parol evidence rule is applicable. As Justice Riley (as he then
was) noted in
Wong
:

[240]  Of course, where an oral contract is
alleged the [parol] evidence rule necessary[ily] operates differently than it
would in the case of a written contract. As Justice Adair explained in
Shaw
Production Way Holdings v. Sunvault Energy, Inc.,
2018 BCSC 926
at para.
151
,
aff’d
2019 BCCA 72
, “the interpretation of oral contracts turns on the same
essential principles” that govern written contracts, however “in the case of a
completely oral contract there is greater flexibility in the nature of the
evidence that is admissible to prove the contents of the contract and the
meaning of the language used by the parties”. This “follows intuitively” from
the recognition that oral contracts must often be construed without the benefit
of a written instrument by which the parties expressed their respective rights
and obligations in mutually agreed upon language.

[241] To prove
any contract, oral or written, the plaintiff must establish on a balance of
probabilities that the parties reached a legally binding agreement. The test is
“whether parties have indicated to the outside world, in the form of the
objective reasonable bystander, their intention to contract and the terms of
the contract”:
Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church of Canada St. Mary
Cathedral v. Aga
,
2021 SCC 22
at para.
36
[
Ethiopian Orthodox
Tewahedo Church
], citing G.H.L. Fridman,
The Law of Contract in Canada
,
6
th
ed. (Toronto: Thomson Reuters, 2011), at 15.

[
207
]

A trust is not a separate legal entity but is rather a legal
relationship. The choice of a trust as an investment vehicle determines the
attendant rights and responsibilities of the trustee and the beneficiaries.

[
208
]

With respect to a contract to create a trust,
Waters’

Law of Trusts

characterizes it in the following manner at 67–69:

Agency arises out of contract, trust out of
conveyance and the fiduciary obligation of the transferee. This we have already
seen when examining the relationship of agent and trustee. When we turn to the
concepts of contract and trust, we are obviously looking at the same matter but
from a different and broader angle. Contract is a vehicle for the creation of
reciprocal obligations between the parties to an agreement; the parties
exchange value with each other. Contract is therefore essentially bargain, and
in the common law system, unlike the civil law, contract by definition excludes
gift, a transfer under which no value is given by the recipient. The object of
a contract may take the form of a sale or exchange of property. However, while
value or consideration is a broad concept, it does not include a promisee’s
reliance upon the promise to his or her detriment. As we have seen, a trust is
a mode of transfer of property:  the transfer may come about as a result of
contract, or it may be a gratuitous unilateral act. That is to say, the settlor
or testator may make a gift of property  to others by way of a trust whereunder
the donees become beneficiaries, or the beneficiaries or a third party may
supply value or consideration to the settlor or testator in return for his or
her promise to create the trust and the transfer or property to it. The latter
is a contract to create a trust.

However, whether or not the trust is the
outcome of contract, once it is created, whether by will or
inter vivos
act,
and the property has been effectively transferred to the trustees, it is fully
enforceable by the beneficiaries against the trustees.

The terms that
are enforceable must also be identified. If the trust was created as the result
of a contract, and whether or not the documentation includes a specific “Trust
Agreement”, the terms of the trust will be found in the contract itself,
further to which the trust agreement, possibly and, if so, unwisely expressed
in differing language, was drawn. That is to say, though the terms of the trust
should be exactly and comprehensively reproduced in the trust agreement, the
court is free in the event of doubt or silence to consult the language of the
contract. The contractual agreement is the found and origin of the trust, and
this may result in the court looking at any or all of the documents that
contain evidence of the agreement reached.

[
209
]

Where a contractual relationship is established between the parties,
care must be taken to ensure that “the interpretation of either facts or
documents must not be distorted or given undue emphasis in order to impose the
existence of a trust, where a reasonable and impartial interpretation would
reveal that such a trust was neither intended nor created”:
Zeitler v. The
Estate of Alfons Zeitler
,
2008 BCSC 775
at para.
70
.

[
210
]

The onus of proof as to the existence of a valid trust lies with the
person asserting it:
Larochelle v. Soucie Estate
,
2019 BCSC 1329
[
Larochelle
]
at para.
176
.

[
211
]

A bare trust arises when a trustee simply holds legal title to an
asset, with all of the risks and rewards remaining with the beneficial owner. A
bare trustee must deliver the trust property to the beneficiary upon demand:
Dediu
v. Martin Estate
,
2023 BCSC 852
[
Dediu
] at para.
100
. A
distinguishing characteristic of a bare trust is that the trustee has no
independent powers, discretions or responsibilities, and his or her only
responsibility is to carry out the instructions of the beneficiaries:
Scoretz
v. Kensam Enterprises Inc.,
2018 BCCA 66
at para.
33
. For the purpose
of this proceeding only, the parties acknowledge that the oral trust (as set
out in the Agreement) and the subsequent written trust deeds are not bare
trusts. This is a proper admission for the purpose of this proceeding, and I
will proceed on that basis.

[
212
]

If, as in these circumstances, the oral agreement is to create a trust,
the evidence must establish both a declaration of trust and constitution of the
trust:
Larochelle

at para.
176
. The declaration of the trust
requires three essential characteristics known as the three certainties:
certainty of intention to create the trust, certainty of the subject matter of
the trust, and certainty of the trust object:
Warde v. Slatter
,
2017
BCSC 274
at para.
12
. It is not necessary for the trust to be set out in a
written document: it may be construed from conduct, or from documents and
conduct taken together. The constitution of the trust requires the transfer of
title to the trust property to the trustee:
Larochelle

at para.
177
.

[
213
]

Certainty of intention to create the trust is
analyzed with the intention of the parties as at the time of the transaction:
Virk
BCCA

at para.
51
. Certainty of intention may be inferred from a
consideration of all the surrounding circumstances. As Justice Donegan (as she
then was) noted in
Larochelle
,
there is no need for any specific
technical words or expressions:

[183] Certainty of intention requires that
the settlor’s intention to create a trust must also be established with
certainty in order for a trust to be valid. The settlor must clearly intend the
recipient to hold the property in trust. While a trust can be construed from
conduct alone, words are generally necessary to show intention. However, there
is “no need for any technical words or expressions for the creation of a
trust”:
Waters’ Law of Trusts
at 141. Conversely, the use of the terms
“trust” and “trustee” in the originating document are probative, but not
determinative, of the intention to create a trust:
Angus v. Port Hope (Municipality)
,

2017 ONCA 566
(Ont. C.A.) at para.
104
.

[184] Evidence
to determine the settlor’s intention is not limited to the originating document.
External evidence may be taken into account to resolve ambiguities, or “where
the extrinsic evidence clearly demonstrates that the words of the document do
not reflect the intention of the parties”:
Waters’ Law of Trusts
at 143.
In fact, courts have characterized a search for certainty of intention that is
limited to the document alone as a “vacuous inquiry”:
Antle v. R.,
2009
TCC 465
(T.C.C.[General Procedure]) at para. 44 (aff’d
2010 FCA 280
(F.C.A.)
).

[
214
]

Certainty of the subject matter of the trust requires certainty of
the property subject to the trust, and certainty of the beneficiary’s interest
in that trust property:
Grewal v. Khakh
,
2018 BCCA 357
at para.
26
.

[
215
]

Finally, certainty of the object of the trust requires that the
objects of the trust must be clearly delineated, and there must be no
uncertainty as to whether an individual is, in fact, a beneficiary:
Dediu

at paras.
101–102
.

2.

Analysis

[
216
]

As set out above, in the section entitled “Brief Background”, the
parties are largely in agreement on the events in 1996 surrounding the purchase
of the Property.

[
217
]

I am satisfied that Mr. Mand and Mr. Gill
introduced the Property to Mr. Cheema. Mr. Cheema purchased the
Property for $690,000.00 in September 1996. The parties agree that around the
time Mr. Cheema purchased the Property they reached the Agreement. That is,
that Mr. Cheema would hold legal title to the Property in trust for the
beneficial owners of the Property, being: Mr. Mand as to a 10% beneficial
interest, Mr. Gill as to a 10% beneficial interest; and Mr. Cheema as
to an 80% beneficial interest.
The parties also agree that the terms of that Agreement were:

a)

Mr. Mand and Mr. Gill were to pay Mr. Cheema their
respective 10% capital contribution for the acquisition of the Property;

b)

Mr. Mand and Mr. Gill were to pay Mr. Cheema their
respective 10% of the ongoing expenses related to the Property;

c)

Mr. Mand and Mr. Gill were responsible for renting out the
Home; and

d)

Mr. Cheema would hold legal title to the Property pursuant to an
oral trust with the same terms.

[
218
]

While I heard significant evidence on when exactly the parties
reached the Agreement that Mr. Mand and Mr. Gill would be 10%
beneficial owners of the Property—whether before or after the removal of the
subject clause on the contract of purchase and sale—that is not a relevant
issue that must be resolved. The parties all agree the Agreement was reached
before the purchase of the Property completed. Likewise, I heard significant
evidence on when the involvement of Mrs. Mand and Mrs. Gill was first
raised. Notwithstanding Mr. Gill was adamant that it was right from the
beginning, Mr. Mand and Mr. Cheema disagreed with this, and both said
their involvement was first raised in 2005. There is no independent documentary
evidence that can resolve this conflict, and again it is not necessary to do so.

[
219
]

It is clear that neither Mr. Mand nor Mr. Gill disclosed
their beneficial interest in the acquisition of the Property to the vendor of
the Property as required to do pursuant to s. 28 of the
Real Estate
Act.
While Mr. Cheema no longer argues this failure invalidated the
trust, he does say it reflects poorly on their credibility. I agree. Both Mr. Mand
and Mr. Gill testified that they were aware of the disclosure obligations
in force at the time the Property was acquired, and neither offered any clear
evidence as to why they failed to make such disclosure. The only logical inference
is that they decided not to go on legal title, nor on the mortgage, for the
Property because of their concerns about this professional obligation.

[
220
]

There was also significant evidence from Mr. Cheema that the
plaintiffs refused to assume any responsibility for the mortgage on the
Property. I need not resolve if, or why, they refused to do so, but I find that
Mr. Cheema was the sole mortgagor and his son, Rajpal Cheema, guaranteed
the mortgage required for the purchase of the Property.

[
221
]

I find the purchase of the Property completed on September 17, 1996,
with a possession date of September 19, 1996. The amount required for
completion was $385,376.76. The parties agree the capital contribution required
from Mr. Mand and Mr. Gill for their 10% beneficial interest was
$40,537.67 each. Mr. Gill has provided independent documentary evidence to
support his evidence that he paid his 10% share for the capital contribution to
purchase the Property by way of a bank draft dated September 13, 1996 in the
amount of $40,537.67. Mr. Cheema admits Mr. Gill made this payment.

[
222
]

However, while both Mr. Mand, Mrs. Mand
and Mr. Gill maintain Mr. Mand also paid the identical amount, Mr. Mand
has no documentation to support his evidence. I find it to be a reasonable
inference based on the documentary evidence that does exist, the
uncontroversial evidence agreed to by the parties, and the conduct of the
parties in the years that followed, that, in all of the circumstances, Mr. Mand
made his capital contribution. In reaching this determination, I do not rely
upon Mrs. Mand’s evidence that she recalls seeing a significant amount of
money withdrawn from their bank account in 1996, nor on Mr. Mand’s
evidence, but rather on the subsequent behaviour of the parties, which only
makes logical sense if Mr. Mand did in fact make the required payment.
That subsequent behaviour, which is corroborated by documentary evidence, includes:

a)

the cheque register that records a payment from Mr. Mand to Mr. Cheema
on June 30, 2004, in the amount of $2,500.00, with the notation “Subject
Property”, which matches the same payment Mr. Gill made on that day;

b)

Mr. Cheema including Mr. Mand as a named beneficiary on
Trust Agreement #1, Trust Agreement #2 and the Modification Agreement; and

c)

Mr. Mand’s involvement in matters related to the Property after
1996 including:

i.

being a contact with the City of Surrey in 2006
with respect to an application for a commercial building on the Property;

ii.

being a contact with Surrey City Development from 2009 to 2013 with
respect to potential development of the Property and the Land Swap;

iii.

being a contact for Aplin & Martin Consultants Ltd. (“Aplin
& Martin”) from 2010 to 2013; and

iv.

being a contact for a potential development in 2013 at the Property.

[
223
]

While Mrs. Mand corroborated Mr. Mand’s testimony, and
said that when she reviewed their cheque book between 1999 and 2004 she recalls
seeing cheques that had been made payable to Mr. Cheema, I put no weight
on her evidence, given my concerns with her credibility and reliability as set
out below.

[
224
]

However, I also rely upon the fact that Mr. Cheema
clearly gave Mr. Mand and Mr. Cheema financial statements for Transport
Ltd. in 2015 or 2016, for the years ended April 30, 2013 and April 30, 2014,
albeit it in heavily redacted form, and a copy of an appraisal for the Property
obtained in 2016. I address both of these findings of fact in greater detail above
and below, in para. [197] and
[449].

[
225
]

Finally, Mr. Gill testified he was present
and observed Mr. Mand present his bank draft, in the same amount as his
own, to Mr. Cheema. The plaintiffs say Mr. Gill was not challenged on
this evidence, although Mr. Cheema denies Mr. Mand did so. I do not
find it would appropriate to rely on the rule in
Browne v. Dunn
to accept
Mr. Gill’s evidence on this point as the plaintiffs suggest.

[
226
]

While I accept that Mr. Cheema did not have
an email address and, therefore, relied on friends and family to accept and
send emails on his behalf, I do not find Mr. Cheema’s explanation that Mr. Mand
would just “come along” to the meetings as his friend to be credible or
logical. Neither do I accept his evidence that Mr. Mand was some kind of a
consultant or assistant for him, and that he agreed to behave as such in the
hope of getting further business from Mr. Cheema.

[
227
]

Further, Mr. Cheema’s evidence on this
point has changed significantly over the course of the litigation. At his
examination for discovery on January 23, 2023, he did not deny that Mr. Mand
had paid his capital contribution. Rather, he said:

570   Q    Mr. Cheema, I’m asking you if you –for your
recollection. Did Gary Mand pay you an equivalent amount of around –over
$40,000 for the purchase of the 152
nd
Street property prior to the
closing?

A     I do not remember if he had given. If given, then he
can show me the records, because Kuldip has also shown.

…

573   Q    And I’m not referring you to any document today. I’m
asking for your recollection.

A     Honestly I do not remember. If given, if there’s any
record, he can show me.

…

575   Q    You don’t deny that Mr. Mand provided you with that
money, do you?

A
I answered earlier. I do not know whether he gave me
or not. Deny is different. He can prove.

[Emphasis
added.]

[
228
]

However, at trial, his evidence changed; he was
adamant that Mr. Mand had not made the capital contribution, and that he
specifically recalled not only that fact but confronting Mr. Mand about that
in 2005. He did not tender a satisfactory explanation at trial to explain the
significant difference in his evidence. I do not accept this self-serving
evidence to be true; rather, I find it is an ever-changing narrative that Mr. Cheema
came to as a result of his position in highly adversarial litigation that evolved
as the issues between the parties came to be framed more clearly.

[
229
]

Accordingly, I am satisfied that the parties entered into the Agreement
before the completion of the purchase of the Property, and agreed that Mr. Cheema
would hold legal title to the Property in trust for the three beneficiaries,
being Mr. Cheema as to an 80% interest, Mr. Mand as to a 10%
interest, and Mr. Gill as to a 10% interest. The Agreement was subject to
the terms set out at para. [217] above.

[

[26]  It is helpful at this point to
consider the distinct origins of trust and contract law. Whereas contracts stem

Waters’ Law of Trusts in
Canada

th

One system of
law was interpreted and moulded in the King’s Courts, and another system of law
was gradually being established in the Lord Chancellor’s Court, ultimately
called the Court of Chancery. The first is the common law in the strict sense,
the second is Equity, a gloss upon the first
,
designed as an act of the King’s residual justice to bring equity to bear in
the application of the laws of the realm. Equity is superior in authority
because it is the King’s personal ruling concerning the application of “his”
justice in the realm. Equity, like the common law, gradually became
institutionalized, with each system using its own forms and procedure, but
in
matters of substance Equity assumed the existence of the common law, assisting,
modifying, and supplementing it.

…

It was out of
this unique state of affairs
, which enured even to
the point of separately administered systems until the latter half of the
nineteenth century,
that the trust was born.
In the eyes of the common
law courts if [the trustee] held the legal title to land or chattels, he had
the rights of disposition, management and enjoyment of that property. But, if
[the trustee] had earlier promised the transferor to hold the property for the
enjoyment of a person other than [the trustee] himself,
the Court of
Chancery was asked and finally agreed to enforce the moral obligation. At law,
[the trustee] might be owner in the fullest sense that the common law
recognized ownership, but in equity – which [the trustee] could not avoid if he
were summoned to account [ B, the intended beneficiary, could compel [the
trustee] to yield up the enjoyment in the property and indeed administer it on
B’s behalf.
[Emphasis added/]

the common law is sometimes described by the maxim “equity follows the law”: J.
McGhee, ed.,
Snell’s Equity
, 31
st

Where a rule,

its circumstances, or the particular point, a court of equity is as much bound
by it as a court of law, and can as little justify a departure from it.

However, the maxim that equity follows the
law does not mean that common law always trumps equitable doctrines. To the
contrary,
s.44
of the
Law and Equity Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 253,
provides that equity prevails where the rules of law and equity conflict.

[28] These statements may at first appear

relationship between equity and the common law is contextual. …

[Emphasis in
original.]

name. As Justice Fenlon noted in

Krypt, both the contract and the oral
trust are “indissociable”: at para. 31. The nature of the legal
arrangement the parties chose, in order to implement their investment in the

the contract may be the original of the trust, the contractual terms cannot
eliminate the fiduciary obligations of the trustee.

[

The law is settled that Mr. Cheema, in his capacity as Trustee,
was a fiduciary. As such he owed fiduciary obligations to the beneficiaries of
the trust. Those obligations may be found both in the common law and the
equitable law of trusts. Some of those obligations were codified in the
Trustee
Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 464 [
Trustee Act
], which came into force
some seven months after the oral trust was entered into, on April 21, 1997.

[

Much has been written about fiduciary obligations owed by trustees,
which is not necessary to canvas in depth here. However, I am satisfied that Mr. Cheema,
in his capacity as Trustee, owed the beneficiaries the duty to follow the terms
of the oral trust, and to observe those general principles of trust law which
did not run counter to the express terms of the Agreement and the oral trust. These
fiduciary obligations were neither contracted out of by the parties, nor
minimized by the business arrangement entered into by the parties. He also owed
the following duties, which are relevant to the analysis of the issues before
me:

a)

the duty to exercise the care, diligence and skill of a reasonably
prudent person;

b)

the duty to act honestly, in good faith, and in the best interests
of the beneficiaries;

c)

the duty of loyalty, which requires a trustee not to act in the face
of a conflict, not to prefer their personal interest, and not to take a secret
profit, act dishonestly, or in bad faith;

d)

the duty to act impartially, and not to prefer one beneficiary or
group of beneficiaries to another;

e)

the duty to avoid self-interest where their interest could conflict
with the interests of the beneficiaries;

f)

the duty to act in accordance with the settlor’s
intention and purpose in creating the trust, and to comply with the terms of
the trust instrument or trust arrangement;

g)

the duty to preserve the trust property on behalf of the
beneficiaries;

h)

the prohibition against acting in a manner that would give rise to a
conflict of interest, except with the informed consent of all beneficiaries
(the “no conflict rule”);

i)

the prohibition against personally profiting
from the trust (the “no profit rule”); and

j)

the duty to maintain adequate records and to
account to the beneficiaries for the trust property.

Alexander,

previously taken or now sought. A passing of accounts application is the
opposite of remedial; it is a process that seeks a court order that no remedy
is necessary with respect to the accounts: see Furrow and Zacks, at pp. 9-10.
Thus, the passing of accounts does not fit within the first part of the
Limitations
Act, 2002
definition of claim.

[28]  An application for the passing of
accounts also does not fit within the second part of the statutory definition
of claim. Where the definition speaks of an act or omission, it must surely
refer to an action taken or not taken by a third party that has the effect of
causing loss, injury, or damage. It would be a strange result if a limitation
period could not be triggered until the party asserting the claim took an
action or omitted to do something.

[29]  The
result, in my view, is that a passing of accounts under the
SDA
is
not subject to the two-year general limitation period found in the
Limitations
Act, 2002
. The common law in that regard was not changed with the
enactment of that legislation. Consequently, the only defences available
are the equitable defences of laches and acquiescence, neither of which were
asserted in the present case.

[
274
]

The
SDA
referred to in this quote is the
Substitute
Decisions Act
, 1992, S.O. 2002, c. 30. I find the analysis equally
applicable to a trustee seeking approval of their reasonably incurred expenses,
and I am not persuaded by the plaintiffs’ argument.

[
