]

However, in oral submissions, the plaintiffs
agreed the focus of their submissions were on the equitable doctrines of laches
and proprietary estoppel. The defendants agreed the focus of their submissions
was that their position should not be defeated by the application of either
doctrine. This applied to both the time period from 1996 to March 30, 2005, and
to the subsequent time period.

[
276
]

The parties agree that the doctrine of laches requires equitable
claims be prosecuted without undue delay to do justice between the parties.
There is no set time period after which the doctrine will apply. Rather, the determination
requires consideration of all of the circumstances and, in particular, the
length of the delay and the nature of the acts of the parties during the period
of delay. A determination that the delay amounts to laches requires a
consideration of (1) the claimant’s acquiescence to the state of legal affairs
and (2) a change in position by the respondent arising from reasonable reliance
on the claimant’s acceptance of the status quo:
Manitoba
Métis Federation Inc. v. Canada (Attorney General),
2013 SCC 14
[
Manitoba Métis Federation
]

at para.
145
.

[
277
]

Acquiescence depends on knowledge, capacity and
freedom:
Manitoba Métis Federation
at para.
147
. Acquiescence as to
the state of legal affairs requires a party to have knowledge of their rights,
and to know their rights give rise to an equitable claim. Acquiescence arises
where a claimant delays, with full knowledge of the existence of their rights,
and a breach of their rights, which leads to the inference of waiver:
M.(K.)
v. M.(H.)
, [1992] 3 SCR 6,
1992 CanLII 31 (SCC)
[
M.(K.)
] at 78–79. As
the Supreme Court of Canada explains in
M.(K.)

at 78–79:

Acquiescence is a fluid term, susceptible to
various meanings depending upon the context in which it is used. Meagher,
Gummow and Lehane, supra, at pp. 765-766, identify three different senses,
the first being a synonym for estoppel, wherein the plaintiff stands by and
watches the deprivation of her rights and yet does nothing. This has been
referred to as the primary meaning of acquiescence. Its secondary sense is as
an element of laches – after the deprivation of her rights and in the full
knowledge of their existence, the plaintiff delays. This leads to an inference
that her rights have been waived. This, of course, is the meaning of
acquiescence relevant to this appeal. The final usage is a confusing one, as it
is sometimes associated with the second branch of the laches rule in the
context of an alteration of the defendant’s position in reliance on the
plaintiff’s inaction.

As the primary
and second definitions of acquiescence suggest, an important aspect of the
concept is the plaintiff’s
knowledge
of her rights. It is not enough
that the plaintiff knows of the facts that support a claim in equity; she must
also know that the facts give rise to that claim:
Re Howlett
,
[1949]
Ch. 767
. However, this court has held that knowledge of one’s claim is to be
measured by an objective standard; see
Taylor v. Wallbridge
(1879),
1879 CanLII 1 (SCC)
, 2
S.C.R. 616, at p. 670. In other words, the question is whether it is
reasonable for a plaintiff to be ignorant of her legal rights given her
knowledge of the underlying facts relevant to a possible legal claim.

[
278
]

Chief Justice McLachlin (as she then was) set
out the test for proprietary estoppel in
Cowper-Smith v. Morgan
,
2017
SCC 61
:

[15]  An equity
arises when (1) a representation or assurance is made to the claimant, on the
basis of which the claimant expects that he will enjoy some right or benefit
over property; (2) the claimant relies on that expectation by doing or
refraining from doing something, and his reliance is reasonable in all the
circumstances; and (3) the claimant suffers a detriment as a result of his
reasonable reliance, such that it would be unfair or unjust for a party
responsible for the representation or assurance to go back on her word. […]

[
279
]

The representation need not be an express statement, but may be
implied by conduct or a course of conduct. The representation or assurance must
be clear, and intended to have been taken seriously:
van Dishoeck v. Centre
Stage Holdings Ltd.,
2023 BCSC 1500
at paras.
198–199
.

1.

Applicable Legal Principles

[
382
]

I invited the parties to address the legal principles of conditions
precedent and conditions subsequent within the context of a trust deed. The
defendants addressed this legal issue while the plaintiffs did not.

[
383
]

The intention of the parties is to be analyzed
at the time the transaction was entered into:
Virk BCCA

at para.
51
.
As Justice Watchuk noted in
Mong Alter Ego Trust No. 1. v. Yip
,

2022 BCSC 1327
:

[104] The
court’s task is to “construe the agreement against the background facts to
determine objectively the ‘aim’ of the transaction”. In doing so, the court
must look at all of the circumstances, not just the words of the trust deed:
Larochelle

at para.
193
(citing
Mohr v. C.J.A.
(1991), 40 E.T.R. 12
(B.C.C.A.)
).

[
384
]

I have considered these legal principles already in my analysis of
whether there was an oral trust, and in my analysis of the trust deeds entered
into by the parties.

[
385
]

The parol evidence rule provides that, subject to certain
exceptions, when the parties to an agreement have set down all of the
agreements’ terms in a document, extrinsic evidence is not admissible to add
to, subtract from, vary or contradict those terms:
Gallen v. Butterley,
53
BCLR 38,
1984 CanLII 752 (BC CA)
at para.
34
.

Among the exceptions
are evidence to demonstrate the factual matrix of the agreement, to establish a
collateral agreement, or to support an allegation that the document itself was
not intended by the parties to constitute the whole agreement: at para. 35;
see also
Thomson v. Thomson Estate
,
2024 BCSC 2039
[
Thomson Estate
]
at para.
32
.

[
386
]

If a provision requiring interpretation is ambiguous, following
consideration of its text and the factual matrix surrounding the creation of
the contract, post-contracting performance of contractual obligations can be
admitted “as an aid to interpretation of the agreement in question”:
Thomson
Estate

at para.
58
.

[
387
]

Within the trust context, Justice Newbould noted in
Computershare
v. Crystallex
,
2011 ONSC 5748
:

[20]  A trust
indenture is a contract and normal principles of contract interpretation apply
to its construction. In interpreting a contract, the goal is to determine the
intent of the parties by reference to the words that they chose. The plain
meaning of the words is to be given effect, read harmoniously and in the
context of other provisions of the contract, and in light of the factual matrix
as a whole. Interpretations that give effect to all the terms of a contract
should be preferred over interpretations that render one or more terms
superfluous or ineffective. A commercial contract should be interpreted in a
manner that accords with sound commercial principles, good business sense and
that does not result in absurdities.

[
388
]

With respect, I cannot agree that a trust is a contract. For the
reasons set out above at para. [200], a trust is a legal relationship,
which arises when a person is compelled to hold title to property for the
benefit of others (of whom he may be one). When a trust relationship is a
component of a contractual relationship
, then the two
cannot be dissociated, as Justice Fenlon
noted in
N-Krypt
.
The
inability to dissociate the two does not lead to the trust being found to be a
contract. Rather, the court must consider the fiduciary obligations owed by the
trustee in that capacity, and the contractual obligations agreed to by the
parties, both within the context of the commercial arrangement. The choice by
the parties to utilize the vehicle of a trust as part of the commercial
arrangement requires an assessment of both the obligations of the trustee, and
those of the parties to the contract—neither can be ignored.

[
389
]

A condition precedent is a term in a contract requiring a specific
event or occurrence to happen, which if it does not take place, allows the
contract to be treated as repudiated:
1061403 B.C. Ltd. v. Canada Willingdon
Holdings Ltd.,
2018 BCSC 1067
at para.
53
. There are two types of
conditions precedent: a “true” condition precedent and an “internal” condition
precedent. A “true” condition precedent requires a third party to fulfil the
condition whereas an “internal” condition precedent is one which can be
satisfied by the actions of the parties: at paras. 54–56. If an “internal” condition precedent is
not satisfied, then the other party has the choice of either repudiating the
contract, or affirming it: at para. 55. Put another way, with a condition
precedent, no gift under a trust is intended until the condition is fulfilled.
Such a gift is contingent, and the condition must be fulfilled for the gift to
be vested:
Jack Estate (Re)
,
2019 BCSC 777
[
Jack Estate
] at para.
28
.

[
390
]

A condition subsequent differs, in that “non-compliance with the
condition will put an end to an already existing gift”:
Canada Trust Co. v.
Ontario (Human Rights Commission)
, [1990] CarswellOnt 486,
1990 CanLII 6849
(ON CA)
at 20. Such a gift is characterized as one vested, subject to divestment:

Jack Estate

at para.
28
.

[
391
]

As noted in
Waters’

Law of Trusts
at 337–338:

Finally, one of
the common causes of failure of conditions is that they are uncertain. If a
condition fails for uncertainty, the question of whether it will also fail for
public policy reasons does not have to be decided. This has occurred in a
succession of English cases commencing with
Re Borwick
in 1993 involving
possible restraint on freedom of religious allegiance. Conditions requiring
persons to be openly and avowedly Protestant, or to conform to the Church of
England, or not to marry any person not of Jewish parentage and of the Jewish
faith have failed for uncertainty. These were cases involving conditions
subsequent, and the test the courts apply in such a situation is that it must
be clear from the moment of the commencement of the interest “precisely and
distinctly upon the happening of what event” it is that the interest is to be
divested.

…

Behind this diction between conditions
subsequent and precedent lies the fact that the courts are not anxious to
strike down a gift if that can be avoided. The condition subsequent, being
void, leaves the gift free to run its natural duration. In this respect, the
courts are assisted by the presumption of early vesting, for this means that
there is a presumption in favour of a condition subsequent rather than a
condition precedent.

Not every condition subsequent will be one
which is subject to divestment.

responsibility of ensuring the share of the liabilities of the Beneficiaries

paying their respective shares owing. The fiduciary
obligations of Mr. Cheema, both pursuant to the oral trust component of
the Agreement, and later pursuant to the terms of Trust Agreement #1 and #2,

records for the Property, but was also seeking regular reimbursement from the
plaintiffs for the expenses of the Property.

[

Given this, I cannot find that the plaintiffs breached a condition
subsequent, such that their entitlement as beneficiaries was divested. For such
a condition subsequent to be found, it must either be clearly set out within
the terms of the trust deed itself, or clearly found to be the intention of the
parties at the time. Such a condition subsequent would have to not only
identify the obligation, and who bore the responsibility of calculating the
amount owed, but also the consequence of non-compliance. It would have to
clearly set out upon what event the beneficial interest was to be divested. There
is no evidence such a condition subsequent was part of the Agreement, nor within

finding that it can be found from the intentions of the parties at the time
they entered into the Agreement. There is no basis upon which to conclude that Mr. Cheema

to divestment, that could result in the termination of the Agreement. Mr. Cheema,
in his capacity as Trustee, cannot hide behind a failure to provide the
beneficiaries with an accounting of their proportionate share of expenses, and
a failure to seek their proportionate contribution, and then rely upon their
failure to make such payment to argue their beneficial ownership should be
divested as a result. He was, and is, a fiduciary, and in that role, was
required to put forward an accounting upon which to seek their proportionate
contribution. His proper remedy is in seeking an accounting and payment of
their respective proportionate share of expenses.

[

Likewise, to the extent the plaintiffs argue that they never
approved the expenses of Mr. Cheema as Trustee in writing, the fact is
they never sought details of the expenses he was incurring. They cannot now
argue that they are not responsible for their proportionate share.

Although neither party argued the issue, I note

Re Vince Insurance Trust
,

at para.
29

[28]  It is helpful to start by summarizing
the legal principles applicable to a trustee's claim to be indemnified for
trust-related expenses.

[29]  Trustees are
entitled to be indemnified against all reasonable costs
and expenses they incur as trustees:
Geffen v. Goodman
Estate,
1991 CanLII 69 (SCC)
, [1991] 2 S.C.R. 353. This is reflected
in
s. 95
of the
Trustee Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 464,
which provides, in material part, that a trustee "may reimburse himself or
herself, or pay or discharge out of the trust premises,
all expenses incurred in or about the execution of his or her trusts
or powers".

[30]  The general test to
determine whether an expense is properly incurred, and therefore
recoverable, is described in Donovan W.M. Waters, Mark R. Gillen & Lionel
D. Smith,
Waters' Law of Trusts in Canada
, 4th ed. (Toronto:
Thomson Reuters Canada Limited, 2012) at 1209 as:

whether
the expense incurred arose out of an act within the scope of the
trusteeship duties and powers, whether in the circumstances it was reasonable,
and whether it was something that his duty as the trustee required him to do.

[31]  The application of
this test, generally speaking, would disentitle a trustee to indemnification
for expenses arising out of his or her own misconduct:
Tebbs
v. Carpenter
(1816), 1 Madd. 290, and expenses that he or
she voluntarily assumed:
Waters' Law of Trusts
at 1210. The
matter is more complicated, however, in cases where a strict application of the
test would preclude indemnity but where the trust benefited from the
incurred expense.

[32]  It has been observed
that in such circumstances, it would be reasonable "to indemnify the
trustees on the ground that the beneficiaries are unjustly enriched":
Albert H. Oosterhoff, "Indemnity of Estate Trustees as Applied in
Recent Cases" in Megan Connolly & Anne E.P. Armstrong eds,
Ontario
Estate Administration Manual
, (Toronto, Thomson Reuters Canada) (WL). Similarly,
the authors of
Lewin on Trusts
, 17th ed. (London: Sweet &
Maxwell, 2000) at 539, express the view that where a trustee has acted in good
faith and has incurred costs in a transaction benefiting the trust estate, he
or she may be entitled to indemnification even where the transaction was
unauthorized:

In general, a
trustee is not entitled to indemnity if he incurs costs or liabilities in a
transaction which is unauthorised and without the request or
implied
assent
of the beneficiaries
.
However, if the trustee acts in good
faith, and the transaction benefits the trust estate, he may be entitled to
indemnity to the extent that the transaction benefits the trust estate, though
whether the indemnity is a matter of right rather than of discretion of the
court is not clear.

[Emphasis added]

[33]
Ultimately, what is regarded as a properly incurred and therefore
recoverable expense is "a question of fact in the circumstances
of each particular case":
Waters' Law of Trusts
at
1209. The applicable principle I draw from the foregoing authorities is that
there is no absolute prohibition against the indemnification of a trustee
for expenses incurred as a result of acts beyond the scope of the
trust (including voluntary acts) in circumstances where the denial of indemnification
would result in unjust enrichment of the beneficiaries.

The Court of Appeal set out a useful summary of

Pirani v. Pirani
,

[

noting none of these propositions are controversial:

[94] The parties agree on a number of
incontrovertible general principles. First, trustees are fiduciaries and owe
duties to the beneficiaries of the trust. Second, as a general matter, trustees
should not act in the face of a disabling conflict of interest or duty. Third,
conflicts may exist between duties owed as trustees, and duties owed in other
capacities; or conflicts may exist between duty and interest. Fourth, where a
trustee acts in the face of a disabling conflict, the trustee will bear the
onus of demonstrating that decisions were taken in good faith within the scope
of the trustee’s powers. Depending on the circumstances, the trustee may also
have to demonstrate they did not profit from acting as a trustee. Fifth, a
prima facie conflict may arise where there is a substantial risk the conflict
could sway the decision making.

[95] The parties also agree these general
propositions are context specific, and not necessarily of universal
application. Their applicability turns, at least in part, on the extent to
which the trust instrument, interpreted in its appropriate factual matrix,
informs, alters, modifies, or displaces the scope and content of fiduciary
duties. The parties agree the trust instrument may authorize a trustee to act
in the face of what may otherwise be a disabling conflict; displace the
operation of the “no profit” rule; and in other ways modify the content of the
fiduciary duty, for example, displacing an obligation to act only in the best
interests of all beneficiaries with a more limited duty.

[96] It is also
common ground that in order to establish the degree to which the trust
instrument has modified a trustee’s duties, it is necessary to seek to
determine the actual intentions of the settlor. This inquiry involves
interpreting the trust agreement in light of the context in which the trust was
established, its purposes and the principles governing its administration.

1.

Applicable Legal Principles

[
451
]

In
Pirani
,

the Court went on to note that when a trust
is created, trustees may be authorized to act in the face of a conflict, and
may also be relieved of other aspects of their fiduciary duty: at para. 102.

[
452
]

The plaintiffs rely on the principles of equitable compensation, and
say they are entitled to their proportionate share of the rental income Mr. Cheema
ought to have received for the Property, had he rented it to an arm’s-length
lessee.

[
453
]

Equitable compensation is a loss-based remedy, intended to deter
wrongdoing and enforce the trust at the heart of fiduciary relationships:
Southwind
v. Canada
,
2021 SCC 28
[
Southwind
] at para.
66
. It differs from
an accounting for profits or a constructive trust, both of which are gain-based
remedies, meant to measure a fiduciary’s gain rather than a plaintiff’s loss.
Rather, equitable compensation is a loss-based remedy, intended to make up the
plaintiff’s loss: at para. 67. The Supreme Court of Canada characterizes
it as “equity’s counterpart to common law damages”: at para. 69. It is
discretionary and restitutionary in nature, and aims “to restore the actual
value of the thing lost through the fiduciary’s breach, referred to as the
plaintiff’s lost opportunity”: at para. 69. To find equitable compensation
appropriate, there must be factual causation; that is, the fiduciary’s breach
must have caused the plaintiff’s lost opportunity: at para. 70.

[
454
]

At its heart, equitable compensation “…is designed to put the
beneficiary in as good a position financially as he or she would have occupied
but for the breach of the equitable obligation, not a better one”:
Shen v.
West Continent Development Inc. (BC0844848),
2020 BCSC 5
at para.
98
.

[
455
]

Equity is especially concerned with deterring
wrongful conduct by fiduciaries, as beneficiaries are peculiarly vulnerable to
a fiduciary’s use, misuse or abuse of power. As
Southwind

explains, “[b]y
restoring the beneficiary’s lost opportunity, equitable compensation enforces
the fiduciary relationship and deters the fiduciary’s wrongful conduct”: at para. 72.
The Court in
Southwind

also states:

[73]  Due to these differences, rather than
relying on common law principles, McLachlin J. explained that the proper
approach to equitable compensation “is to look to the policy behind
compensation for breach of fiduciary duty and determine what remedies will best
further that policy” (
Canson
, at p. 545). McLachlin J.’s approach
was subsequently followed by this Court in
Cadbury Schweppes Inc. v. FBI
Foods Ltd.
,
1999 CanLII 705 (SCC)
, [1999] 1 S.C.R. 142, and recognizes that
the applicable rules will depend both on the nature of the fiduciary
relationship and the fiduciary obligations: “Differences between different
types of fiduciary relationships may, depending on the circumstances, dictate
different approaches to damages” (
Canson
, at p. 546). In other
words, “[t]he rules appropriate to a breach of duty by a trustee . . . have to
be determined in the light of the characteristics of the obligation in
question” (
AIB
, at para. 93). There must be a close relationship
between the fiduciary duty and the fiduciary remedy, and the fiduciary duty
must “forcefully shape the content of [the] fiduciary remed[y]” (
Bray
,
at p. 451). Thus, while factual causation will always apply to equitable
compensation in the sense that the fiduciary’s breach must cause in fact the
plaintiff’s loss, common law limiting factors will not readily apply because of
the nature of the fiduciary relationship and obligations.

[74]  Equity assesses the loss at the date
of trial and with the benefit of hindsight (
Guerin
, at pp. 361-62,
per Wilson J.;
Canson
, at p. 556;
Target Holdings Ltd. v.
Redferns
,
[1996] 1 A.C. 421 (H.L.), at pp. 437-39)
. This means that
equity compensates the plaintiff for the lost opportunity caused by the breach,
regardless of whether that opportunity could have been foreseen at the time of
breach. McLachlin J. described the analysis as follows:

The plaintiff’s
actual loss as a consequence of the breach is to be assessed with the full
benefit of hindsight. Foreseeability is not a concern in assessing
compensation, but it is essential that the losses made good are only those
which, on a common sense view of causation, were caused by the breach.

(
Canson
, at p. 556)

[75]  McLachlin J.’s use of the phrase
“common sense view of causation” in
Canson
should not be taken to mean
that the causation analysis in equitable compensation cases will always have an
“intuitively obvious answer” (
AIB
, at para. 95). This is not always
the case; trial judges are often faced with difficult questions of causation in
claims for equitable compensation. Instead, the phrase “common sense” clarifies
that the rules developed in legal causation, such as foreseeability, do not
readily apply in equity: “The requirement that the loss must result from the
breach of the relevant equitable duty does not negate the fact that ‘causality’
in the legal sense as limited by foreseeability at the time of breach does not
apply in equity” (
Canson
, at p. 552). Professor Rotman explains the
same point as follows:

Each starts with
the idea of “but for,” “cause-in-fact,” or “sine qua non,” causation. This
generally satisfies Equity, but the common law requires more; it demands a
finding of materiality or substantial cause to link the impugned activity with
the harm to the plaintiff. Further, the common law imports ideas of
foreseeability (or reasonable contemplation) and remoteness into its assessment
of causality. . . . These other considerations do not readily enter into
Equity’s assessment of fiduciary accountability.

(
Fiduciary Law
(2005), at p. 634).

See, also,
Target
Holdings
, where Lord Browne-Wilkinson observed that “the common law rules
of remoteness of damage and causation do not apply” (p. 434).

[
456
]

However, a plaintiff must establish that their
losses flowed from the breach of fiduciary duty:
Stirrett v. Cheema
,

2020 ONCA 288
[
Stirrett
] at paras.
86–90
.

[
457
]

Further, to achieve the purpose behind equitable
compensation, “the assessment is also guided by presumptions that equity makes
against breaching fiduciaries”:
Southwind

at para.
78
.
One such presumption is that “[e]quity presumes that the
plaintiff would have made the most favourable use of the trust proper
ty”:
at para. 79. However,
Southwind
makes clear:

[80]  The focus is always on whether the
plaintiff’s lost opportunity was caused in fact by the fiduciary’s breach.
Equity will assess that opportunity under the
presumption
that the
beneficiary would have put the asset to its most favourable use. The most
favourable use must be realistic. The common law requires a plaintiff to lead
evidence to that effect.

[81]  There are additional equitable
presumptions that are applicable in appropriate cases. The presumption of
legality, discussed in more detail below, prevents breaching fiduciaries from
reducing compensation by arguing they would not have complied with the law.

[82]  Another presumption, the so-called
Brickenden rule, applies where the fiduciary breached a duty to disclose
material facts. The breaching fiduciary is prevented from arguing that the
outcome would be the same regardless of whether the facts were disclosed (
Brickenden
v. London Loan & Savings Co.
,
1934 CanLII 280 (UK JCPC)
, [1934] 3
D.L.R. 465 (P.C.)).

[83]  In
summary, equitable compensation deters wrongful conduct by fiduciaries in order
to enforce the relationship at the heart of the fiduciary duty. It restores the
opportunity that the plaintiff lost as a result of the fiduciary’s breach. The
trial judge must begin by closely analyzing the nature of the fiduciary
relationship so as to ensure that the loss is assessed in relation to the
obligations undertaken by the fiduciary. The loss must be caused in fact by the
fiduciary’s breach, but the causation analysis will not import foreseeability
into breaches of the Crown’s fiduciary duty towards Indigenous Peoples.
Equitable presumptions — including most favourable use — apply to the
assessment of the loss.
The most favourable use must be
realistic.
The trial judge must be satisfied that the assessment reflects
the value the beneficiary could have actually received from the asset between
breach and trial and the importance of the relationship between the Crown and
Indigenous Peoples.

[
458
]

Ultimately, equitable compensation “is a discretionary remedy that is
assessed and not precisely calculated”: at para. 123. Rather, as the Court
explains, “a trial judge will often have to provide a global assessment of the
lost opportunity and that assessment needs to be realistic”: at para. 123.
The Court has the discretion to fashion an appropriate remedy. Equitable relief
is “flexible, adaptable, and intended to address fairness between the parties
and the integrity of the fiduciary relationship”:
Sather Ranch Ltd. v.
Sather
,
2024 BCSC 598
at para.
44
.

Section 99

Trustee Act

codifies what was once a common
law duty of a trustee to present and pass their accounts. When a trustee and
beneficiaries are unable to reach a consensus on the trustee’s proper accounts,
then those accounts must be brought before the court for a resolution. Rules
25-13 and 25-14 of the
Supreme Court Civil Rules
provide a procedural
code for doing so. Specifically, Rule 25-13(3)(b) provides that the court may
direct the Registrar “to conduct an inquiry, assessment or accounting in
relation to any matter relating to the accounts or the remuneration of the
personal representative”. Rule 25-13(3)(c) provides the court may “make any
other order or give any direction that the court considers appropriate in the
circumstances”. Further, upon referral of the matter to the Registrar, then
under Rule 25-13(5), unless the court otherwise orders, the Registrar must
certify his or her results in Form P39. If a Form P39 certification is filed
under Rule 18-1(9), then the certificate is binding, subject to appeal, on the
persons who had notice of the inquiry, assessment or accounting.

of the
PPA

sets out who may
bring a proceeding for partition:

Parties to proceeding and persons
entitled to notice

4 (1) Any person
who, if this Act had not been passed, might have maintained a proceeding for
partition may maintain such a proceeding against any one or more of the
interested parties without serving the other or others, and a defendant in the
proceeding may not object for want of parties.

[
518
]

This section codifies the test for standing set
out in
Morrow v. Eakin
, [1952] 2 D.L.R. 593,
1953 CanLII 278 (BCSC)
at
594–595. The test has been
described as “whether a party could have brought the partition application
under English law as it existed in 1858”:
Chung v. Chung
,
2018 BCSC 1126

[
Chung 2018
] at para.
35
, citing
Pallot v. Douglas
,
2017
BCCA 254
[
Pallot
] at para.
17
.

[
519
]

The Court of Appeal in
Pallot

approved
the following description of who was entitled to bring a petition for partition
under English law in 1858:

[20]  A recent summary as to who was entitled to bring a petition
for partition under English law in 1858 is found in the British Columbia Law
Institute consultation paper
Consultation Paper on the Partition of
Property Act
(June 2011) at 5-6:

In order to determine who is eligible to seek partition,
therefore, the English law pre-dating the English
Partition Act
,
1868 [31 & 32 Vict., c. 40] needs to be examined. Specifically, it is
the law of England as it existed on 19 November, 1858 that needs to be
examined, as the
Law and Equity Act
[R.S.B.C.
1996, c. 253, s. 2] makes English law as it existed on that date
applicable in British Columbia except to the extent it has been altered by laws
of the province or is inapplicable to local circumstances. As of that date, the
classes of persons eligible to seek partition were coparcenary tenants and
those co-owners to whom the statutes of 1539 and 1540 had extended the remedy.
As coparcenary tenancy no longer exists, the persons eligible to seek partition
or sale in lieu of partition in British Columbia are those described in the
1539 and 1540 statutes, namely:

(a) joint tenants of the fee simple or a profit à prendre;

(b) tenants in common of the fee simple or a profit à prendre;

(c) joint tenants or tenants in common of a life estate;

(d) co-owners of a leasehold estate (co-lessees).

There is another requirement: anyone seeking partition or sale
must have an immediate right to possession of the land.

Thus owners of a future interest, such as joint tenants of a remainder
following a life estate, cannot claim these remedies.

[Emphasis
added.]

[
520
]

The issue of who has standing to demand
partition or sale of property under the
PPA

was addressed by Justice
Pearlman in
Chung 2018
. He considered both the Court of Appeal decision
in
Pallot
,
as well as the trial decision (
Pallot
v. Douglas
,

2015 BCSC 1296
). He concluded:

[47] If, upon an
examination of the terms of the trust, there is a bare trust and the
beneficiary is entitled to conveyance of the legal title to the property, then
the beneficiary has an immediate possessory interest. Conversely, if the trust
gives management and control to the trustee, the beneficiary cannot demand
partition and thereby vary the terms of the trust:
Pallot v. Douglas
,

2015 BCSC 1296
at para.
37
.

[
521
]

Section 6
of the
PPA

provides:

Sale of property where majority requests
it

6  In a
proceeding for partition where, if this Act had not been passed, an order for
partition might have been made, and if the party or parties interested,
individually or collectively, to the extent of 1/2 or upwards in the property
involved request the court to direct a sale of the property and a distribution
of the proceeds instead of a division of the property, the court must, unless
it sees good reason to the contrary, order a sale of the property and may give
directions.

[
522
]

Section 7
of the
PPA

sets out the process
by which the Court may order a sale instead of a partition:

Sale in place of partition

7  In a proceeding for partition where, if
this Act had not been passed, an order for partition might have been made, and
if it appears to the court that because of the nature of the property involved,
or of the number of parties interested or presumptively interested in it, or of
the absence or disability of some of those parties, or of any other
circumstance, a sale of the property and a distribution of the proceeds would
be more beneficial for the interested parties than a division of the property,
the court may

(a)

on the request of any of the interested parties
and despite the dissent or disability of any other interested party, order a
sale of the property, and

(b)

give directions.

[
523
]

Where a party or parties hold less than a 50
percent interest in the property, the effect of
s. 7
places the burden on
them to establish why a sale and distribution of proceeds would be more
beneficial to the interested parties than a partition of land:
Zackariuk v.
Chepsiuk et al
,
2005 BCSC 919
[
Zackariuk
] at para.
33
.

[
524
]

Finally, s. 8 of the
PPA

provides a
right of first refusal to any party interested in the property where an order
for sale is made, to allow a party to purchase the share of the party
requesting the sale:

Purchase of share of person applying for
sale

8 (1) In a proceeding for partition where,
if this Act had not been passed, an order for partition might have been made,
then if any party interested in the property involved requests the court to
order a sale of the property and a distribution of the proceeds instead of a
division of the property, the court may order a sale of the property and give
directions.

(2)The court may not make an order under
subsection (1) if the other parties interested in the property, or some of
them, undertake to purchase the share of a party requesting a sale.

(3) If an
undertaking is given, the court may order a valuation of the share of the party
requesting a sale in the manner the court thinks fit, and may give directions.

[
525
]

Justice Smith provided a very helpful summary of
the application of these sections in
Zackariuk
:

[27]  In
Harmeling v. Harmeling
,
1978
CanLII 1961 (BC CA)
, [1978] 5 W.W.R. 688 (B.C.C.A.), the court considered what
is now s. 2 of the Act. At ¶ 10 it stated:

I think that we ought to accept without
qualification the general statement that there is a prima facie right of a
joint tenant to partition or sale and that the Court will compel such partition
or sale unless justice requires that such an order should not be made.

[28]
Harmeling
involved an
application for an order for sale by a joint tenant under the equivalent of
s. 2 of the Act. That section applies equally to any co-owner, tenant in
common, or party who has an interest in land.

[29]  Section 2 provides the gateway through
which a party with an interest in land may have the court consider whether to
order a partition or sale of the property. A party who does not wish to “suffer
partition or sale” bears the onus of demonstrating to the court that justice
requires that the order for partition or sale not be made. Failing such a
demonstration, the court must enforce the interested party’s
prima facie

right to partition or sale.

…

[32]  Having met the s. 2 threshold,
the court must next consider the application of ss. 6 and 7 of the Act in
dealing with the court’s discretion to order partition or sale.

[33]  Where a party or parties requesting an
order for sale hold a 50% or greater interest in the property, s. 6
requires the court to grant an order for sale instead of a partition, unless
the opposing party or parties establish “good reason” why such an order should
not be made. Where a party or parties hold less than a 50% interest in the
property, s. 7 places the burden on the party or parties to establish why
a sale and distribution of the proceeds would be more beneficial to the
interested parties than a partition of the land. See
Hoggard v. Hoggard
,

[1996] B.C.J. No. 2502 (S.C.)
.

[34]  A number
of cases cited by both the petitioner and the respondent, while distinguishable
on their facts, demonstrate the strength of the
prima facie
right of a
co-owner to compel sale. In each of the cases sale was ordered because the
opposing party could not demonstrate that justice required no order be made. They
also demonstrate that partition, or actual division of the land as opposed to
sale, is a rare order. [citations omitted]

2.

Analysis

[
526
]

The defendants argue that the plaintiffs are not entitled to an
order for partition and sale. The plaintiffs were surprised by this position in
closing argument and argued that not only was the position wrong at law, but to
make such an argument at this stage was an abuse of process. They grounded this
argument in the fact that the defendants withdrew this legal position from
their response to civil claim filed in July 2020, after receiving a letter from
counsel for the plaintiffs dated July 30, 2020 asking them to reconsider this
position and confirming that, if they did not do so, the plaintiffs would apply
for further declaratory relief and would make a formal demand for transfer of
legal title (which would inevitably cause double property transfer tax to be
payable). After receipt of this letter, the defendants withdrew the allegations
that the plaintiffs lacked standing under the
PPA

in their amended
response to civil claim filed on August 19, 2020.

As I agree the
defendants’ position is wrong at law, it is not necessary that I consider the plaintiffs’
argument that their position in closing submissions was an abuse of process.

[
527
]

The defendants argue that beneficiaries of a trust, under which trust
property is owned, do not have standing under the
PPA

as they do not
have a right to an immediate possession of trust property. They argue that they
must first dissolve the trust pursuant to the rule known as the “rule in
Saunders
v. Vautier”
from the 1841 English decision which provided that if all beneficiaries
are
sui juris
and in agreement, they may terminate a trust and have the
trust property transferred to them:
Pallot

at paras.
36–37
.

[
528
]

However, Trust Agreement #1 provided the beneficiaries with the
ability to demand Mr. Cheema transfer legal title to the Property “to or
as directed by the Beneficiary forthwith upon the written demand of the
Beneficiary”: clause 2(d). As already noted, “Beneficiary” is a defined term in
the trust deed, meaning all of the named beneficiaries. The same provision is
found in Trust Agreement #2.

[
529
]

I am satisfied that, pursuant to the terms of the trust deed, the
plaintiffs are entitled to demand Mr. Cheema convey legal title to the
Property to them as to their 20% beneficial interest, and thus, have an
immediate possessory interest. That provides them with the necessary standing
to seek an order for partition and sale pursuant to the
PPA
.

[
530
]

In the alternative, were I persuaded by the defendants’ argument
that the plaintiffs lacked standing, I would have granted the plaintiffs a
vesting order pursuant to the terms of the trust deed, much as Justice Grauer
(as he then was) did in
Haigh v. Kent
,
2016 BCSC 333
[
Haigh
] at para.
15
.

[
531
]

The burden is on the plaintiffs, as they hold less than a 50 percent
interest in the Property, to establish why a sale and distribution of the
proceeds would be more beneficial than a partition of the Property:
Zackariuk
,
at para.
33
. I am satisfied that the plaintiffs have satisfied this
burden. To continue to tie the parties together as co-owners of the Property by
way of partition would just generate further conflict and inevitable legal
proceedings. The most efficient manner in which to address the high level of
conflict and animosity between the parties is to order the sale of the Property.

[
532
]

At trial, the plaintiffs tendered an expert report of Ms. Fenton (“Fenton Appraisal”), qualified to give appraisal
evidence in British Columbia, who opined that as of October 5, 2022, the market
value of the Property was $24,000,000.00. Her opinion noted that the Property
is currently zoned A-1 (General Agriculture Zone), is designated “Mixed
Employment” in the Official Community Plan, and is designated as “Business
Park” in the East Newton Business Park Neighbourhood Concept Plan. She provided
an appraisal of the Property at its “Probable Highest and Best Use” for
development to a business park.

[
533
]

In their opening submissions, the plaintiffs indicated they would be
willing to accept an offer to purchase their 20% beneficial interest for
$4,800,000.00, being 20% of the fair market value as set out in the Fenton
Appraisal. However, otherwise, they say the Trust Property should be sold on
the open market for fair market value, and they should receive 20% of the net
sale proceeds, plus equitable damages.

[
534
]

Notwithstanding that the defendants cross-examined Ms. Fenton
at length on the assumptions underlying her opinion, and were highly critical
of her decision to appraise the Property at its “Probable Highest and Best Use”
without considering the cost and time delay of re-zoning the Property, they
failed to tender their own appraisal.

[
535
]

In closing argument, for the first time in a year and a half, Mr. Cheema
advised he wishes to buy out the plaintiffs, should they be found to still have
a beneficial interest in the Property. However, s. 8(2) of the
PPA

provides
the Court may not order a sale if another party with interest in the property
undertakes to purchase the share of the party requesting the sale. Mr. Cheema
has not made such an undertaking. It is only if such an undertaking is given
that the Court may order a valuation of the share of the party requesting a
sale in the manner the Court thinks fit:
Haigh

at para.
56
.

[
536
]

It would be neither proportionate, nor efficient, after 108 days of
trial, to deny the plaintiffs the relief they seek, and prolong the litigation
between the parties. I am satisfied the plaintiffs have established they are
entitled to the order they seek—that the Property be sold. I will address in further detail below
how the net sales proceeds from the sale of the Property are to be divided.
